## 1. Reason for Referral and Evaluation Questions

### 1.1 Referral concerns

Nicolás was referred for a bilingual speech-language evaluation because his family and preschool staff reported difficulty understanding directions, explaining needs, and producing clear sentences. His mother described frequent reliance on pointing when a listener did not understand him. His father reported that conversations often stopped after an initial request.

The referral requested information about communication across Spanish and English. It also requested recommendations for treatment and classroom support. The evaluation addressed whether the reported difficulties reflected differences in language exposure, an underlying communication disorder, or both.

### 1.2 Scope and sources

This assessment combined parent interviews, preschool observations supplied by staff, record review, structured tasks, and play-based sampling. Information about development came from caregivers unless a reviewed record is identified.

The clinician completed the evaluation in Spanish and English. No interpreter participated. Conclusions reflect the child's performance during this appointment and the information available at the time. The report does not establish an educational eligibility decision.

## 2. Background and Referral Records

### 2.1 Previous services

The family first contacted Briarfen Children’s Developmental Services Agency after concerns about early vocabulary development. The assigned service coordinator, J. Ortiz, helped arrange developmental screening and parent coaching.

An earlier IFSP dated November 16, 2024 included outcome 1.2, which addressed requesting help during household routines. Outcome 2.1 addressed participation in shared play with a caregiver. Those services ended when the child transitioned from the infant-toddler program.

A transition summary from Briarfen CDSA described increased use of gestures and single words. It also documented continued difficulty combining words without adult support. The summary did not include a bilingual diagnostic assessment.

### 2.2 Community supports

The family reported contact with Briarfen County DSS for transportation information and benefit renewal assistance. The child receives nutrition support through Briarfen County WIC. The family also attended a parent workshop offered by Briarfen Smart Start.

Earlier home visits through Lantern Reach Early Head Start focused on responsive play and predictable routines. These agency contacts provide context for service access. They do not independently establish the presence or severity of a language disorder.

The current referral packet included preschool notes, a pediatric summary, and the prior transition record. No previous comprehensive speech sound evaluation was available.

## 3. Birth, Developmental, and Medical History

### 3.1 Pregnancy and delivery

His mother reported an uncomplicated pregnancy until elevated blood pressure developed near delivery. Birth occurred at Cedar Lantern Regional Hospital at 38 weeks, 2 days gestation. Reported birth weight was 6 pounds, 11 ounces.

Apgar scores were 8 at the first recorded interval and 9 at the second recorded interval. The parent recalled routine observation after delivery without intensive care admission. Feeding began with breast milk and later included formula.

The family reported no prenatal exposure concerns and no major delivery complications. These statements reflect caregiver history rather than direct review of the complete birth record.

### 3.2 Developmental milestones

Independent sitting reportedly emerged at 7 months, walking at 14 months, and the first consistent spoken word at approximately 18 months. Word combinations appeared around 30 months.

The family described steady development without a clear loss of previously acquired skills. Toilet learning remains inconsistent during unfamiliar routines. Dressing and mealtime participation improve when adults demonstrate the expected action.

### 3.3 Hearing and medical status

The pediatric provider, Dr. Mara Ellison, documented recurrent middle-ear fluid in a referral note dated September 18, 2026. The family reported several ear infections but no ear tube placement.

A hearing screening at Cedar Lantern Regional Hospital on September 24, 2026 was recorded as passed. The available summary did not provide detailed thresholds or tympanometry results.

There was no reported history of seizures, major injury, chronic respiratory disease, or swallowing concerns. The child takes no daily medication according to his parents. Sleep varies when congestion increases. Current hearing access remains relevant because intermittent middle-ear problems can affect listening during language learning.

## 4. Family, Caregiving, and Language History

### 4.1 Household and caregivers

Nico lives with his mother, Lucía Beltrán, his father, Daniel Mercer, and his older sister, Sol Beltrán. His maternal grandmother, Teresa Valdés, provides care on some afternoons.

A family babysitter, M.R., assists during occasional evening work shifts. The household has a dog named Canela. Family members reported that the child frequently initiates play involving the dog.

His father works at Pineglass Packaging Cooperative. His mother works at Juniper Ledger Market. Work schedules sometimes change the available caregiver, but the family described stable routines for meals and bedtime.

### 4.2 Language exposure and use

Spanish has been used with the child since birth. English exposure increased after preschool enrollment at 3;1. His mother and grandmother primarily use Spanish. His father uses both languages, and his sister generally uses English during pretend play.

Caregivers estimated that current home interactions occur in Spanish approximately 65% of the time and English approximately 35%. These estimates describe exposure and are not direct measurements.

The child selects language according to the activity and partner. He often uses Spanish for comfort and familiar requests. English appears more often during songs, classroom routines, and play with peers. Mixed-language utterances were reported and observed.

### 4.3 Relevant family history

His mother reported that an uncle, Esteban Valdés, received childhood speech therapy. The family did not know the diagnosis or treatment duration.

During picture naming, the target word "sol" referred to the sun. His sister's name, Sol, has the same spoken form. Naming the picture was scored as a vocabulary response, separate from identifying a family member.

## 5. Preschool Participation and Functional Communication

### 5.1 Classroom setting

The child attends The Tumbleglass Lantern, a mixed-age preschool program in Larkhaven. His lead teacher is Ms. Amina Rosales. Classroom support is provided by Mr. Jonah Pike.

Staff reported that he participates readily in movement songs, snack routines, and familiar construction play. He has more difficulty during group discussion, unfamiliar transitions, and activities that require a spoken explanation.

His teacher described him as observant and socially interested. He frequently watches another child before beginning a task. This strategy helps participation but can conceal difficulty understanding the original direction.

### 5.2 Peer interaction

He commonly plays beside Mila Chen and Owen Price. Staff reported that he follows their play themes but rarely explains a new idea without adult support.

When a peer takes a desired object, he may pull the object back, point, or call an adult. Staff have begun modeling short request phrases. They reported better success when the phrase matches an immediate need.

### 5.3 Classroom language demands

Preschool instruction occurs primarily in English, with Spanish support during selected routines. Visual schedules and demonstrations are available. Staff reported that directions involving location words, sequence, or several objects create the greatest difficulty.

The classroom report was consistent with parent concerns. Both settings described stronger communication during predictable routines than during unfamiliar verbal tasks.

## 6. Assessment Procedures and Behavioral Observations

### 6.1 Procedures

The clinician used PLS-5 Spanish, selected items from GFTA-3, a bilingual language sample, and informal dynamic assessment. The informal measures included the Conceptual Vocabulary Probe, Direction-Following Probe, and Dynamic Sentence Learning Probe.

Structured testing alternated with play, movement, and brief breaks. Spanish and English prompts were selected according to task requirements and observed comprehension. Caregiver information supported interpretation of unfamiliar vocabulary.

### 6.2 Participation

The child entered the room with his mother and initially remained close to her. He explored the toys after the clinician demonstrated a familiar play routine. Engagement improved when activities had a clear purpose and a visible ending.

He tolerated table tasks for brief periods. Attention decreased during extended verbal instructions. Repetition, gestures, and object demonstrations improved participation. No major distress or refusal occurred.

### 6.3 Interpretive limits

Several standardized items required additional explanation, alternate-language prompts, or teaching. These changes departed from standardized administration. The score table therefore preserves protocol-derived values for descriptive documentation, but those values cannot support valid normative conclusions.

Language exposure, task familiarity, attention, and possible fluctuating hearing access also affect interpretation. The clinician placed greater weight on communication across settings, bilingual sampling, error patterns, and response to teaching.

The assessment supports a clinical formulation. It does not provide an isolated numerical measure of the child's overall ability.

## 7. Test Results and Language Findings

### 7.1 Score table

The following values were recorded during the assessment. Standardized values are descriptive because administration changes affected comparability with the normative sample.

| Measure | Subtest or task | Raw score or accuracy | Standard score | Percentile | Age equivalent | Confidence interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish | Auditory Comprehension | 39 | 76 | 5th percentile | 3;1 | 90% interval: 70–84 |
| PLS-5 Spanish | Expressive Communication | 37 | 74 | 4th percentile | 2;11 | 90% interval: 68–82 |
| PLS-5 Spanish | Total Language | 76 | 73 | 4th percentile | 3;0 | 90% interval: 67–81 |
| Conceptual Vocabulary Probe | Naming across languages | 18/30; 60% | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| Direction-Following Probe | Familiar directions | 8/10; 80% | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| Dynamic Sentence Learning Probe | Sentence expansion after teaching | 7/10; 70% | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable |

Age equivalents describe performance on selected items. They do not represent a developmental age or determine treatment placement.

### 7.2 Receptive language

On Auditory Comprehension, the child identified familiar objects and actions with greater success than relational concepts. He understood routine requests when the relevant object was visible.

He followed unfamiliar directions containing a location contrast on 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Performance decreased when the direction required retaining several pieces of information without visual support.

He showed emerging understanding of simple questions about actions. Questions about reasons, future events, and sequence required demonstrations or choices. Similar difficulty appeared in both languages, although familiar Spanish vocabulary improved access.

### 7.3 Expressive language

On Expressive Communication, the child used words for requests, labels, refusals, and comments. Spontaneous utterances usually contained short combinations. Sentence structure became less stable when he described an event beyond the immediate setting.

Observed productions included "mamá mira carro", "I want ese", and "no cabe aquí". These examples showed meaningful communication and flexible use of available vocabulary.

English productions sometimes omitted grammatical elements. Spanish productions also showed limited sentence expansion and inconsistent verb marking. The presence of difficulty across languages supported concern beyond differences in English exposure alone.

### 7.4 Dynamic learning

Before teaching, he expanded a basic action description on 2/10 opportunities. After modeling and supported practice, performance increased to 7/10 with mod cues.

He retained the practiced structure in a new play activity on 4/10 opportunities with min cues. This response suggests useful learning potential and continued need for guided practice.

## 8. Speech Sound Production, Oral Mechanism, and Voice

### 8.1 Speech sound observations

Selected GFTA-3 items were used to elicit English consonants. No standardized articulation score was calculated because bilingual considerations and administration changes limited normative interpretation.

The child produced several early consonants consistently. Errors included omissions in consonant clusters and variable production of /k/, /g/, and Spanish /ɾ/.

In connected speech, he sometimes used [t] for /k/. One elicited production was "tat" for the target "cat". Spanish words also showed occasional syllable reduction.

A familiar caregiver understood approximately 85% of sampled utterances with context. The clinician understood approximately 65% without caregiver explanation. These estimates reflect this sample and listener context.

### 8.2 Stimulability and movement

The child imitated /k/ in isolation on 3/5 attempts with max cues. Accuracy decreased when the sound was placed in words.

Visible oral structures appeared adequate for the tasks completed. Lip closure, tongue movement, and jaw stability supported eating history and speech participation. The assessment did not identify a clear motor speech pattern, although further observation is warranted.

### 8.3 Voice and fluency

Voice quality was functional during the appointment. Loudness varied with excitement. No persistent strain or unusual resonance was observed.

Brief repetitions occurred when he attempted longer messages. They did not include visible tension or avoidance. Current observations do not establish a fluency disorder.

## 9. Play, Social Communication, and Interaction

### 9.1 Strengths

The child shared attention, brought objects to adults, and checked a listener's reaction during enjoyable activities. He used gestures with words and accepted reciprocal turns when the activity was clear.

Pretend play included feeding a toy animal and placing figures in a vehicle. He extended a familiar play sequence after an adult model.

### 9.2 Areas of need

Communication repair remained limited. When misunderstood, he often repeated the same form or increased his volume. He seldom added a useful detail without support.

Conversation was strongest around visible objects. He needed help maintaining a topic when the listener asked an unfamiliar question. Language limitations appeared to restrict participation despite clear social interest.

The clinician recommends interpreting interaction alongside language demands. This evaluation alone does not resolve broader developmental questions. Persistent concerns across settings should be discussed with the pediatric provider.

## 10. Clinical Impressions

### 10.1 Language formulation

The available evidence supports a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, ICD-10-CM F80.2. Relevant findings include difficulty understanding unfamiliar directions, limited sentence expansion, and reduced ability to explain events across Spanish and English.

Bilingual exposure is part of the child's communication history. It does not adequately explain the full pattern of difficulties observed. This conclusion rests on converging functional evidence rather than the descriptive standardized values alone.

### 10.2 Speech formulation

Speech sound errors reduce clarity and support a speech sound disorder formulation, ICD-10-CM F80.0. Treatment should distinguish developmentally expected patterns and language differences from errors that affect both languages or limit participation.

### 10.3 Prognosis and priorities

Prognosis for functional improvement is favorable with consistent intervention and caregiver participation. The child showed social motivation, responsiveness to models, and measurable improvement during supported learning.

The main priorities are understanding everyday language, producing useful sentences, repairing communication breakdowns, and improving speech clarity. Hearing follow-up remains an important supporting action.

## 11. Recommendations and Proposed Treatment Goals

### 11.1 Direct intervention

Recommend individual speech-language therapy twice weekly for an initial treatment block, subject to authorization and family scheduling. Treatment may be billed under CPT 92507 with modifier GN.

The clinician should provide intervention in Spanish and English according to the child's needs and communication partners. Family members should continue using languages they speak comfortably.

Use focused stimulation, recasts, and play-based practice. Selected principles from Hanen may support caregiver coaching. A Cycles approach may be considered if repeated sampling confirms suitable speech sound patterns.

### 11.2 Proposed goals

1. Follow functional directions containing an action and a location concept on 8/10 opportunities with min cues.
2. Produce an expanded sentence to request, describe, or comment on 8/10 opportunities with mod cues, then reduce support.
3. Repair a communication breakdown by adding a word, gesture, or description on 4/5 opportunities with min cues.
4. Produce selected speech targets in meaningful words on 80% of opportunities with mod cues.
5. Demonstrate carryover of a practiced communication strategy during a familiar routine on 3 of 5 observed opportunities.

### 11.3 Home and preschool support

Adults should gain attention before speaking, use short meaningful directions, and pause for a response. Pair new vocabulary with objects, pictures, and actions. Expand the child's message without requiring repeated correction.

At The Tumbleglass Lantern, staff should preview unfamiliar activities and offer clear language models during peer play. Ms. Rosales can record brief examples of successful requests and communication breakdowns.

Practice should remain connected to daily activities. Caregivers can describe actions during meals, dressing, and shared books. They should accept appropriate responses in either language.

### 11.4 Follow-up

Recommend audiology follow-up if listening concerns or middle-ear symptoms continue. Share this report with the pediatric provider and the family-selected educational team.

A progress review is proposed for January 8, 2027. Repeat assessment should examine functional change and use standardized procedures only when administration conditions support valid interpretation.

## 12. Care Coordination and Report Authentication

### 12.1 Communication plan

With appropriate family authorization, J. Ortiz may help clarify available community supports following the earlier agency transition. Current treatment coordination will occur through WCPCT.

The family may also contact Briarfen Smart Start for local preschool resources. Referral options should reflect actual family priorities and avoid duplicating services.

### 12.2 Family participation

The clinician reviewed the main findings with both parents. They identified clearer requests and better participation in preschool routines as their immediate priorities. They agreed that home practice should fit existing activities.

This report documents a single evaluation encounter. Treatment goals may change as additional language samples and hearing information become available.

Prepared by: Elena Marisol Varela, MS, CCC-SLP  
Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist  
Willow Compass Pediatric Communication Therapy, PLLC  
Electronic signature date: October 10, 2026

Meeting location: Family home

Family information and participation

This review summarizes family participation, communication development, daily routines, and agreed early intervention services. Both parents attended and chose English for the written document. The clinician discussed findings in English and Spanish, checked understanding through teach-back, and invited corrections throughout the meeting. The family uses Spanish during meals, comfort routines, and visits with relatives. English occurs mainly during community activities and care outside the home. The family wants both languages supported.

María Inés del Río Vega lives with her parents and her brother, Tomás Vega del Río, who is 7 years old. Her maternal grandmother, Rosa del Río, provides care on two afternoons each week. An aunt, Beatriz Vega-Solís, helps with transportation when work schedules overlap. The family dog, Mochi, often joins floor play. The parents described these relationships as dependable sources of comfort and communication practice.

The mother works at Copper Finch Textile Cooperative. The father works at Alder Lantern Bicycle Works. Their schedules change monthly, so the family requested flexible visit times with advance notice. Neither parent wants home practice to feel like another appointment. They prefer brief strategies within routines that already happen. The service coordinator confirmed that scheduling requests will go through one contact to reduce repeated calls and missed messages.

Family concerns and priorities in the family's own words

Lucía del Río stated, “I want to understand what she needs before she gets so upset. Sometimes she takes my hand to the cupboard, and I guess wrong. I want her to know that Spanish words count. I do not want anyone telling us to stop speaking the language we use with our family.”

Esteban Vega-Solís stated, “Our biggest priority is an easier supper and an easier goodbye in the morning. We want her to ask for help, show us when she is finished, and enjoy playing with her brother. We can practice during normal life. We cannot make every evening a lesson.”

The family also wants communication partners to recognize gestures, sounds, pictures, and words as valid messages. The parents requested a small set of shared strategies across home and the childcare setting. They want adults to pause before helping, offer meaningful choices, and avoid repeated demands to imitate. They identified participation and reduced frustration as the main signs that the plan is useful.

Developmental and health information

Birth occurred at Crescent Basin Children's Hospital on March 3, 2023. The fictional birth summary lists gestational age as 38 weeks, 2 days, birth weight as 3.12 kg, and Apgar scores as 8 and 9. The parents reported no current feeding restrictions. The pediatrician, Dr. Avery Quill, documented a passed hearing screening on 02-18-2025. These details are included as simulated background information.

The initial developmental visit occurred on el martes 4 de junio de 2024. The first IFSP began on 2024-06-18. At the current review, caregivers described stronger imitation, more frequent shared attention, and better participation when adults follow the child's interests. Transitions remain difficult when an activity ends without warning. No loss of previously used communication skills was reported. The team agreed to monitor hearing, play, and communication through routine follow-up.

Assessment summary

The clinician reviewed the PLS-5 Spanish and its Auditory Comprehension and Expressive Communication subtests. Recorded standard scores were 88 and 79, respectively. The corresponding percentiles were 21st percentile and 8th percentile. The Total Language standard score was 82, with a 90% confidence interval of 77–89. These simulated scores supplement observation and family report; they do not describe every skill across both languages.

During play, Mía followed familiar directions in 8/10 opportunities with gestures and min cues. She selected a named object in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. She used a gesture, picture, or vocalization to request in 60% of observed opportunities. Her productions included "más", "agua", "up", and "no". She produced [w] during an attempt at "water". Speech sampling did not support a separate sound disorder determination.

The clinician observed emerging turn-taking and purposeful communication during familiar activities. Performance decreased when adults introduced several questions in a row. A quieter pace and visible choices improved participation. The family reported more communication at home than during the structured observation. The team therefore selected routine-based outcomes and agreed to compare progress across partners. Language differences and mixed-language utterances will be accepted without correction.

Daily routines: mornings and childcare

Morning care begins around 6:45 a.m.. Dressing is easier when clothing choices are visible and adults announce the next step. Breakfast usually includes fruit, toast, and a drink at the kitchen table. The parents reported that grabbing and crying increase when containers are closed or preferred food is out of reach. The clinician demonstrated a pause, a simple model, and immediate access after any clear communication attempt.

María Inés attends The Copper Teacup Orchard three mornings each week. Teacher Ms. Iris Calderón and classroom assistant Mr. Jonah Reed-Santos described interest in bubbles, toy animals, and the water table. Classmates Alma Chen and Nico Serrano often play nearby. Staff reported that parallel play is comfortable, while sharing a preferred toy requires adult support. The family approved discussion of the agreed strategies with classroom staff.

Arrival occurs near 8:10 a.m.. A predictable greeting and a photograph of the first activity help the goodbye routine. The teacher will acknowledge distress, offer the same brief explanation, and invite a familiar activity. Staff will provide opportunities to request assistance without requiring spoken words. A simple communication board will remain available during snack and play. The family requested that pictures include objects familiar from home.

Daily routines: afternoons and evenings

Afternoon care often includes a walk, a snack, and play on the living room floor. Grandmother Rosa del Río reported that songs and pretend cooking hold attention longer than picture naming. Brother Tomás enjoys building ramps and rolling cars. He will receive simple suggestions for waiting, copying an action, and offering a turn. Adults will supervise and keep his role voluntary. He will not be responsible for managing difficult behavior.

Dinner begins near 6:00 p.m.. The parents want requests for food, help, and finishing to work without repeated guessing. Bath time provides opportunities to choose toys and anticipate familiar actions. Bedtime includes a book, a song, and a short conversation about the day. The family prefers a few repeated words within these routines. They asked adults to respond to the message first and expand language only when the interaction remains comfortable.

Other agencies and community supports

The family receives nutrition support through Alder County WIC Family Center. Contact worker Tessa Bloom helped arrange an appointment for 03/12/2025. The family also uses play materials from Willowbend Smart Beginnings Partnership. No current involvement with Alder County Department of Family Services was reported. The service coordinator will check eligibility for transportation support only if the parents request it. The family identified reliable transportation as a possible future concern.

The sibling attends Juniper Lantern Elementary School. The school does not provide services under this IFSP. The parents requested that appointments avoid school pickup whenever possible. The pediatrician and childcare staff will receive only information covered by the family's documented consent. Interpreter Camila Soto-Naranjo remains available for meetings if the family prefers a separate interpreter. The bilingual clinician will continue to explain clinical terms in plain language.

Outcome 1: communicating needs during meals

By 06/03/2025, during snack or dinner, Mía will communicate a request, refusal, or need for help using a gesture, picture, sign, sound, or word in 4 of 5 naturally occurring opportunities across three routine observations. The family will judge success by less guessing and more comfortable participation. Speech is one possible response. Adults will accept any clear message and will provide the requested item or assistance when available.

Strategies include offering two visible choices, waiting briefly, and modeling "más", "help", or "all done". Adults will use min cues when possible and reduce support as communication becomes more independent. The clinician will coach responsive interaction using principles from Hanen. A picture choice board will be introduced as a practical support. The team is not prescribing a formal PECS protocol. Progress will include caregiver examples and brief observations.

Outcome 2: participating in shared play

By 2025/06/03, during home or classroom play, María Inés del Río Vega will complete a shared sequence with an adult or another child in 3 of 4 opportunities, with no more than mod cues. A shared sequence may include offering an object, waiting, watching a partner act, and taking another turn. The outcome supports participation without requiring eye contact or spoken imitation.

Adults will follow the child's selected activity, copy an action, and introduce one small variation. Models may include "go", "my turn", and "otra vez". Teacher Ms. Calderón will offer short activities with classmate Alma when both children are interested. The clinician will demonstrate how to pause without withholding a needed object. Adults will end the activity when either child shows discomfort. Progress will reflect engagement, successful turns, and the support required.

Outcome 3: making transitions more predictable

By June 3, 2025, during departure or cleanup, María Inés will use or respond to a familiar transition message in 4/5 observed opportunities with min cues. Messages may involve a picture, gesture, object, or word. The family wants adults to recognize requests for help or another moment while keeping the routine predictable. The outcome does not require the child to stop expressing distress.

Strategies include showing the next activity, giving a brief warning, and offering a concrete participation choice. Adults will model "bye", "finished", and "help me". Father Esteban Vega-Solís will practice during the morning goodbye. Grandmother Rosa will use the same picture during afternoon cleanup. The clinician will review whether the support reduces confusion and supports recovery. The team will adjust pictures or wording when a strategy adds demands without helping.

Services, dates, and review plan

Speech-language services through Crescent Heron Therapy will continue from 03/10/2025 through 06/09/2025. The plan provides one home visit each week, lasting forty-five minutes, with caregiver coaching and observation within routines. A monthly visit may occur at The Copper Teacup Orchard with family consent and staff availability. Visits will usually start at 4:30 p.m.. Missed visits will be rescheduled when feasible within the authorization period.

Service coordinator Naomi Bell-Torres will contact the family monthly and arrange the next review. The next planned review is 06.10.2025. Clinician Elena de la Cruz-Méndez will document routine examples, cueing levels, and caregiver feedback after each visit. Notes submitted by CHPC will identify the setting and participating adults. Billing will use 92507 with modifier GN when applicable. The family will receive understandable summaries of progress.

The parents agreed that strategies must fit their schedules and preserve enjoyable interaction. The team will review outcomes sooner if participation changes, a support becomes burdensome, or the family requests a different priority. Both parents confirmed that the document reflects their concerns. The coordinator recorded agreement on 03-03-2025. Copies were designated for the family and authorized team members. NORTH CAROLINA INFANT-TODDLER PROGRAM
INDIVIDUALIZED FAMILY SERVICE PLAN REVIEW
Fictional training document

1. DOCUMENT INFORMATION AND PARTICIPATION

1.1 Review identification

This IFSP review concerns María José Cárdenas Vélez. The review occurred on October 8, 2026, following the initial IFSP dated April 9, 2026. The current service period extends from October 12, 2026 through April 8, 2027. The next scheduled review is January 14, 2027.

The child’s record number is ITP-BW-2604187. The Medicaid member number recorded for this fictional case is 583741926Q. The speech-language service authorization is SLP-261012-0846.

1.2 Participants and language access

Participants included mother Lucía Vélez Duarte, father Andrés Cárdenas Molina, service coordinator Danielle Hartwell, and bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist Elisa Moreno Bell. Interpreter Rosa Vega Cruz supported administrative discussion and interpretation of written consent information.

The family requested discussion in Spanish and an English report. The clinician provided clinical explanations directly in Spanish. The interpreter clarified administrative terms without answering assessment questions for the family. Participants confirmed that the written outcomes reflected their priorities.

2. CHILD AND FAMILY INFORMATION

2.1 Household and contact information

María José Cárdenas Vélez was born on August 8, 2024 and is currently 26 months old. The household includes both parents and brother Tomás Cárdenas Vélez, age 6 years. Maternal grandmother Inés Duarte Salcedo provides care during overlapping work shifts.

The family lives at 1846 Lantern Finch Lane, Alder Creek, North Carolina 27900, in Bellwether County. The primary telephone number is 919-555-0143. The alternate number is 252-555-0186. The preferred email address is l.velez.family@example.test.

The mother grew up in Santa Lucerita del Río, Mexico. Her family’s former mailing address was Calle del Colibrí 27, Barrio Las Jacarandas, Santa Lucerita del Río, Mexico. These details describe family history; they do not indicate another current service location.

2.2 Family strengths and practical needs

The parents share care responsibilities and consistently explain which activities work at home. The father works for Lantern Coast Packaging. His rotating schedule affects meeting availability. The grandmother can join selected home visits with parental permission.

The family has stable housing and reliable telephone access. Transportation requires advance planning. The household dog, Chispa, often participates in play routines and provides a useful reason to request, comment, and take turns.

3. SERVICE COORDINATION AND PARTICIPATING AGENCIES

3.1 Lead office

The lead office is Alder Creek Children’s Developmental Services Agency, located at 620 Meadowglass Avenue, Suite 104, Alder Creek, North Carolina 27900. Its telephone number is 919-555-0128.

Service coordinator Danielle Hartwell will maintain the plan, arrange reviews, confirm provider availability, and help the family obtain accessible notices. The coordinator’s email is dhartwell@aldercdsa.example.test. The office information page is https://aldercdsa.example.test/families.

3.2 Other supports

The family receives nutrition support through River Lantern WIC in Bellwether County. The parents also identified Meadowbridge DSS in Bellwether County as their contact for transportation questions.

With written consent, the coordinator will contact Bright Harbor Partnership for Children in Bellwether County about inclusive community playgroups. These contacts will support access and continuity. They will not replace the services listed in this IFSP.

The family requested one combined contact summary because separate calls during work hours are difficult.

4. DEVELOPMENTAL AND MEDICAL BACKGROUND

4.1 Birth and health history

The parents reported delivery at 38 weeks, 2 days and a birth weight of 6 lb 9 oz. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. A brief feeding observation occurred in the NICU at Soundhaven Health Willowbank Campus Hospital. The reviewed discharge summary did not describe continuing respiratory support.

Pediatrician Dr. Nadia Serrano Pike follows the child at Soundhaven Health Willowbank Campus Pediatric Clinic. The most recent documented well-child visit occurred on September 16, 2026. The parents reported no current daily medication.

4.2 Hearing and related services

Audiologist Owen Bellamy completed a hearing assessment at Soundhaven Health Willowbank Campus Audiology Center on September 23, 2026. The report described responses adequate for access to conversational speech during the assessment.

Occupational therapist Priya Desai Rowan addresses participation in dressing and meals. Physical therapist Marcus Ellison Reed evaluated mobility on September 30, 2026. The team will share functional observations with these providers after confirming the relevant consent.

5. FAMILY CONCERNS AND PRIORITIES

5.1 Family statements

Mother Lucía Vélez Duarte stated: “I understand many things from her face, but other people do not. I want her to tell us what she needs before she cries.”

Father Andrés Cárdenas Molina stated: “At dinner, I want us to know whether she wants more food, a drink, or a break. I also want her to enjoy talking in Spanish with our family.”

Grandmother Inés Duarte Salcedo stated: “When we get ready to leave, she becomes upset. Pictures might help me explain what comes next.”

5.2 Agreed priorities

The family selected functional communication during meals, predictable transitions, and participation with other children. They want strategies that fit existing activities and do not require lengthy practice periods.

The parents value continued Spanish use. They requested support for communication across both languages without pressure to replace Spanish with English. They also want the daycare staff to recognize gestures and emerging words.

The family identified successful communication as being understood through a word, gesture, picture, or combination. Spoken imitation alone is not their main measure of progress.

6. DAILY ROUTINES AND NATURAL ENVIRONMENTS

6.1 Home routines

Breakfast usually begins at 7:15 a.m.. The child chooses between familiar foods by reaching or pointing. Communication becomes harder when several items remain visible but unavailable.

Dressing occurs near 8:00 a.m.. The child participates more readily when an adult offers one garment at a time. The grandmother reported that unexpected changes increase distress.

Dinner begins around 6:30 p.m.. Family members sit together when work schedules permit. Bathing and books follow. The bedtime routine starts at 8:15 p.m.. The parents prefer short shared reading with repeated phrases and opportunities to point.

6.2 Daycare and community routines

The child attends Little Willow Lantern Child Development Center. Teacher Ms. Renata Solís and classroom assistant Bethany Cole support arrival, snack, and outdoor play.

During observation, peer Emilia Navarro offered a toy cup. Peer Noah Bennett joined a rolling-ball activity. The child watched both children and remained nearby. Adults can use these familiar activities to support communication without requiring group performance.

7. ASSESSMENT AND CURRENT FUNCTION

7.1 Sources and interpretation

Speech-language pathologist Elisa Moreno Bell, employed by Juniper Bridge Pediatric Communication Services, completed the review through family interview, routine observation, language sampling, and selected assessment activities.

The earlier PLS-5 administration included Auditory Comprehension and Expressive Communication. Recorded standard scores were 79 and 74, respectively. The recorded Total Language standard score was 75, with a 90% confidence interval of 71–82 and a percentile rank of 5th percentile.

These English-language scores have limited interpretive value for this bilingual child. The team did not use them alone to determine functional needs. Recorded age equivalents of 20 months and 18 months describe test performance and do not represent the child’s overall developmental age.

7.2 Functional communication

During familiar routines, María José followed contextual directions in 8/10 opportunities. Without contextual gestures, responses occurred in 4/10 opportunities. The child independently communicated a request in 3 of 5 snack opportunities.

Observed productions included "agua", "más", and "mama". One sample included "más agua". The clinician recorded an incomplete word using the SALT code [EW]. These observations support functional language intervention and continued assessment across both languages.

8. SPEECH, PLAY, AND PARTICIPATION

8.1 Speech observations

The sample included emerging /m/, /p/, and /b/ productions, documented as /m/, /p/, and /b/. A glide resembling [w] occurred in an attempted word. Productions involving /k/ and /ɾ/ were inconsistent and insufficient for separate treatment targets.

The team will monitor speech development within meaningful communication. It will not require accurate production of every sound before accepting a message.

8.2 Play and regulation

The child enjoys feeding a doll, opening containers, and moving toy animals. Shared play lasts longer when an adult follows the child’s interest and adds a brief model.

Transitions improve when the next activity is visible. During the daycare observation, the child moved from blocks to snack with min cues after seeing a picture. An unexpected move indoors required max cues and direct adult support.

The team will coordinate regulation strategies with occupational therapist Priya Desai Rowan. Communication opportunities will remain brief and responsive to the child’s comfort.

9. IFSP OUTCOME 1: COMMUNICATION DURING MEALS

9.1 Functional outcome and criteria

During meals and snacks, María José Cárdenas Vélez will communicate a choice, request, refusal, or request for help through words, gestures, or pictures. The criterion is 4 of 5 opportunities across three familiar routines, with min cues, documented through family examples and provider observation.

The baseline is independent communication in 3 of 5 snack opportunities, with less consistent communication during dinner.

9.2 Strategies

Adults will place two available items within view, name each item, and allow wait time. They will acknowledge gestures immediately and add a short spoken model.

The clinician will use Enhanced Milieu Teaching, focused stimulation, and recasts during actual meals. Suggested target words include "más", "agua", "ayuda", and "all done". The family may select equivalent words that fit its language use.

Adults will not withhold necessary food or drink to obtain a response. The father will describe successful dinner examples during visits. The teacher will share brief snack observations with parental consent.

10. IFSP OUTCOME 2: PARTICIPATION IN TRANSITIONS

10.1 Functional outcome and criteria

During dressing, daycare arrival, and movement between activities, the child will participate in a predictable transition and communicate acceptance, a request for help, or a request for a brief pause.

Success will occur in 80% of observed transitions across home and daycare, with min cues. The current baseline is 40% with mod cues or greater assistance.

10.2 Strategies

Adults will use visual supports that show the present activity and the next activity. They will offer a short explanation, allow processing time, and acknowledge the child’s message.

Suggested models include "help", "wait", "vamos", and "terminé". Adults will pair spoken language with familiar gestures.

Grandmother Inés Duarte Salcedo will select pictures that match the home routine. Teacher Renata Solís will identify matching classroom pictures. Occupational therapist Priya Desai Rowan will advise on physical comfort and clothing choices when these affect participation.

11. IFSP OUTCOME 3: SHARED PLAY WITH OTHER CHILDREN

11.1 Functional outcome and criteria

During familiar play, the child will initiate or respond to another child through a gesture, sound, word, or shared action. The criterion is 3 of 5 opportunities across two activities with min cues.

The baseline is a response in 1 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. The family wants comfortable participation rather than forced greetings.

11.2 Strategies and review

Adults will arrange simple, repeatable activities such as rolling a ball, feeding dolls, or exchanging toy animals. They will model "my turn", "tu turno", and "mira", then pause.

Brother Tomás Cárdenas Vélez may join when he wishes. His role will remain that of a sibling. At daycare, familiar peers may participate through ordinary classroom play.

The clinician will use caregiver coaching to help adults notice and respond to communication. The team will review progress for outcome 3 through examples from home and daycare, including spontaneous messages and the support required.

12. SERVICES, DATES, AND PROVIDER RESPONSIBILITIES

12.1 Speech-language and related services

Speech-language services will occur once weekly for forty-five minutes in the home, with periodic daycare visits when the family agrees. Services begin on October 12, 2026 and continue through April 8, 2027.

Provider Elisa Moreno Bell will deliver bilingual assessment, intervention, and family instruction. The listed billing code is CPT 92507, with modifier GN. The current diagnostic code is ICD-10 F80.2.

Occupational therapy will occur twice monthly for forty-five minutes through April 8, 2027. Provider Priya Desai Rowan will coordinate dressing and mealtime strategies. Physical therapist Marcus Ellison Reed will provide consultation if mobility concerns affect participation.

12.2 Coordination and scheduling

Service coordinator Danielle Hartwell will contact the family monthly and after any significant service change. The first follow-up contact is scheduled for October 20, 2026 at 4:30 p.m..

Interpreter Rosa Vega Cruz will support administrative meetings when requested. The coordinator will confirm transportation needs before appointments and give the family a clear contact for missed visits.

13. MONITORING, FAMILY AGREEMENT, AND FOLLOW-UP

13.1 Progress review

Providers will record the routine, communication function, level of support, and family interpretation of each example. Brief notes will distinguish independent messages from imitation. Progress will include communication in Spanish and English, gestures, and pictures.

The team will review outcome 1, outcome 2, and outcome 3 at the scheduled meeting. If progress differs across settings, the team will first examine opportunities, language access, comfort, and adult support.

13.2 Agreement and report completion

Mother Lucía Vélez Duarte and father Andrés Cárdenas Molina confirmed that the plan reflects their stated priorities. They requested telephone scheduling and emailed summaries.

The coordinator will distribute the authorized plan and confirm receipt with the family and participating providers. The report was completed on October 9, 2026 by bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist Elisa Moreno Bell.

The next action is to begin the scheduled home visit, confirm useful meal vocabulary, and select transition pictures with the family.

Infant-Toddler Program IFSP Review — North Carolina

This fictional review was completed on September 18, 2026, for Elian Marquez Solano, called Eli at home. His birth date is July 9, 2024, and his age at review is 26 months. The family lives at 7426 Alder Lantern Lane, Brookwillow, North Carolina 27964, in Cedarbend County. The child record number is JT-260918-0472, and the Medicaid member number is 834762915Q. The current service authorization is SLP-26-481730. His mother, Mariela Solano, requests calls at 919-555-0146 after 2:30 p.m. His father, Tomas Marquez, uses 984-555-0182. The family’s shared email is marquez.solano@example.com. Spanish is the main home language. The parents request English documents with Spanish explanations during meetings.

The service coordinator, Ms. Nora Velez, works with Juniper Trace Children’s Developmental Services Agency, also called Juniper Trace CDSA. The office address is 215 Willow Compass Drive, Suite 204, Brookwillow, North Carolina 27964. Its contact number is 919-555-0128, and its family information page is https://junipertrace.example.com/families. I am Camila Rios, MS, CCC-SLP, a bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist employed by River Lantern Pediatric Speech and Language Therapy, PLLC. The family also knows my company as River Lantern Therapy and RLPSLT. I conducted this review in English and Spanish. Interpreter Daniela Moya joined the benefits discussion at the parents’ request.

Family information and priorities

Elian lives with both parents and his sister, Luna Marquez Solano, who is 6 years old. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Solano, provides afternoon care. A neighbor and occasional babysitter, Beatriz Landa, helps when work shifts overlap. The family’s dog, Canela, often sits near the child during floor play. The family previously lived in Aldea Las Nubes del Laurel, near San Jacinto del Cedral, Guatemala. Their former mailing address was Casa 14, Calle del Guayabo, Sector La Loma, Aldea Las Nubes del Laurel. The parents want this hometown recorded because relatives use its name when they describe familiar songs, foods, and family routines.

The parents described several workplaces because their schedules change. Mariela works morning shifts at Cedar Lantern Grocery Store, which she calls Store Cedar Lantern when using Spanish word order with English words. She sometimes covers evening shifts at Blue Fig Restaurant, also called Restaurant Blue Fig. She previously worked for Clear Nest Cleaning Service, which she refers to as Cleaning Service Clear Nest. Tomas works at Stone Reed Packaging Plant, also called Plant Stone Reed. He accepts seasonal work at Copper Meadow Farm, or Farm Copper Meadow, and weekend jobs with High Branch Construction Company, or Construction Company High Branch. These are separate businesses. The family requests flexible scheduling around confirmed shifts.

The mother stated, “I want him to tell me what he needs before he cries. I know his face, but other people do not.” The father stated, “I want to understand him when we eat together. I do not want every meal to become guessing.” Both parents said, “We want Spanish to stay strong. We also want him to understand the people at child care.” Their first priority is requesting food, help, and familiar people. Their second priority is joining short play routines with other children. Their third priority is helping each caregiver respond consistently. They prefer practical activities that fit existing routines and do not require buying special materials.

The reported birth history includes gestational age 38 weeks, 4 days, birth weight 6 pounds, 12 ounces, and Apgar scores of 8 and 9. The mother reported an uncomplicated newborn stay at Willow Lantern Community Hospital. Pediatrician Dr. Adrian Cordero follows growth and general health at Cedarbend Children’s Health Center. Audiologist Leah Duarte completed a hearing assessment on August 21, 2026. The report documented hearing sufficient for access to speech during testing. The family reported no current swallowing concerns. This review does not establish a new medical diagnosis. The existing speech-language treatment diagnosis is ICD-10 F80.2.

Daily routines and assessment

On weekdays, the child usually wakes at 6:45 a.m. Breakfast begins near 7:10 a.m., when the family offers oatmeal, fruit, or toast. He reaches toward preferred food and sometimes pulls an adult’s hand toward the refrigerator. During observation, Eli said "agua" while holding an empty cup and "ma" when offered more banana. His grandmother usually understands these attempts. The father sometimes asks several questions before offering the item. We discussed pausing after one clear choice so the child has time to gesture, vocalize, or use a word. The family selected breakfast as its first practice routine because it happens every day.

Little Orchard Early Learning House provides care on three mornings each week. Arrival is usually at 8:00 a.m., and pickup is near 12:15 p.m. His classroom teacher, Ms. Sofia Beltran, reported that he watches peers before joining. Classroom assistant Mr. Evan Pardo helps him move between activities. He often plays beside Mila Serrano and follows Noah Salcedo toward the block area. During the review visit, he gave a toy bus to Mila after an adult demonstrated the exchange. At home, his sister leads a similar game with cars. The family wants adults to accept his gestures while also offering useful spoken models.

Nap usually begins at 1:00 p.m. Outdoor play follows around 3:30 p.m. Dinner starts near 6:20 p.m., bath time near 7:15 p.m., and bedtime near 8:00 p.m. Transitions become harder when a preferred activity ends without warning. The child responds well when an adult shows the next object and uses the same short phrase. At bath time, the mother will model "wash", "agua", and "all done". At bedtime, the father will pause during a familiar song and accept a sound, gesture, or word as participation. These activities support communication without extending the evening routine.

The initial evaluation occurred on August 28, 2026, from 9:05 a.m. to 10:10 a.m. Assessment included caregiver interview, observation, and selected standardized measures. On the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5), Auditory Comprehension yielded a standard score of 78, 7th percentile, and a 90% confidence interval of 73–85. Expressive Communication yielded a standard score of 72, 3rd percentile, and an age equivalent of 18 months. These scores describe performance under the assessment conditions. They require caution because English norms do not fully represent this bilingual child’s language experience.

The Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale supported a routine-based description across both languages. Skills on Language Comprehension clustered within 18–21 months, with emerging skills within 21–24 months. Skills on Language Expression clustered within 15–18 months. Developmental specialist Iris Calderon previously administered the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition, including Cognitive, on August 14, 2026, and reported a scaled score of 8. The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition and Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fifth Edition were considered but not administered. Limited connected speech and the bilingual assessment needs favored functional sampling.

During play, Elian used "ba", "mama", and "no". A sample contained the SALT code [EW] for an unintelligible word attempt. Observed speech included /m/, /b/, and [w]. Productions of /k/ and Spanish /ɾ/ were not consistent enough to describe. These observations do not establish a speech sound disorder. He followed familiar directions in 6/10 opportunities with min cues and requested through a gesture or vocalization in 4 of 8 opportunities with mod cues. His participation improved when adults followed his interests and allowed a longer response pause.

Outcomes, services, and review plan

Outcome 1: During meals and play, the child will communicate a request using a gesture, word, or word combination in 8/10 opportunities across three consecutive caregiver records. Current performance is 4/10 opportunities. The clinician will use naturalistic language intervention and focused stimulation. Caregivers will place two familiar choices within view, name each choice once, and wait. Useful targets include "more", "mas", "help", and "ayuda". Adults will respond to successful communication and add a short model. Support may begin with mod cues and decrease toward min cues. The family will record examples from breakfast and afternoon play.

Outcome 2: During familiar play, the child will complete three reciprocal turns with an adult or peer in 3 of 5 opportunities. Current performance is 1 of 5 opportunities. Strategies include milieu teaching, expansions, and caregiver coaching drawn from Hanen It Takes Two to Talk. The family will use cars, bubbles, and a ball already available at home. Adults will model "my turn", "your turn", and "otra vez". His teacher will offer the same short routines during classroom play. Direct support may include max cues initially, with planned reduction as participation becomes more independent.

Outcome 3: During transitions, the child will use or respond to a familiar communication signal in 80% of observed opportunities across home and child care. Current performance is 40%. Caregivers will show the next object, give one short direction, and acknowledge protest before guiding the transition. The coordinator will contact Cedarbend Family Nutrition WIC, Cedarbend County Department of Social Services, and Juniper Valley Smart Start about resources the parents requested. Family resource worker Marta Cevallos may help obtain board books. The parents authorized coordination with child care and these agencies through March 17, 2027.

Speech-language services will begin on September 24, 2026, and continue through March 17, 2027. Weekly home visits are scheduled from 4:00 p.m. to 4:45 p.m., with occasional child care visits agreed in advance. The planned billing code is CPT 92507, with modifier GN. Today’s review began at 10:00 a.m. and ended at 11:05 a.m. The next progress review is scheduled for December 18, 2026. The coordinator will confirm work schedules before each visit. Both parents agreed that the outcomes reflect their priorities. They requested continued bilingual coaching and a brief written practice note after each session.

Proposed service period: October 12, 2026 through April 5, 2027

Review participation and purpose

This review addressed communication during meals, play, dressing, and group care. The parents participated throughout the home meeting. The service coordinator joined by telephone. The reporting clinician conducted the visit in English and Spanish according to each participant's preference. This export is written in English. Family statements below preserve the family's wording.

The team reviewed progress, current barriers, and supports that fit existing routines. The parents confirmed that Spanish remains the main home language. English occurs during group care and community activities. The family wants services to support both languages. The team explained that exposure to two languages does not require the family to stop using Spanish.

The child remained nearby during discussion and joined several familiar activities. Participation varied with fatigue and interest. The family could pause the meeting, request clarification, or disagree with recommendations. Both parents helped select the revised outcomes.

Family information and natural supports

Mateo lives with both parents and his sister, Sol. His maternal grandmother, doña Lupe, provides care on some afternoons. A family babysitter, Mr. Tom, occasionally helps when work schedules overlap. The household includes a small dog named Miga. The parents describe the home as active, affectionate, and predictable when adults share the same routine.

Lucía works at Fernwick Orchard Packaging. Daniel works at Copper Finch Cabinet Works. Their rotating schedules make short practice opportunities more useful than separate homework sessions. The family has access to a telephone and can receive printed materials. They prefer brief messages about scheduling and written examples in both languages.

The parents report no current concern about housing or food access. Transportation can be difficult when both adults work. They want advance notice of appointments and permission to include familiar caregivers in coaching. The family identifies shared meals, music, and outdoor play as strengths that can support communication.

Family concerns and priorities in the family's own words

Mother stated, “I know what Teo wants because I watch his hands. Other people do not always understand. I want him to ask before he cries.”

Father stated, “When we get dressed, he runs away if I talk too much. Show me how to give one clear step and wait.”

Mother added, “We want Spanish at home. I do not want my mother to feel that she has to speak English with him.”

Father stated, “At pickup, I hear that he had a hard morning, but I need one example. Was he hungry, waiting, or trying to get a toy?”

The parents' first priority is a reliable way to request help or a preferred item. Their second priority is smoother participation in dressing and cleanup. They also want staff to recognize communication attempts before frustration increases.

The family does not require spoken words for every request. They accept pointing, gestures, pictures, signs, and speech when these methods help the child participate. Mother stated, “If he can show me first, we can build the word later.”

The team agreed to measure progress across ordinary activities. Adults will describe what happened before a communication attempt, what the child did, and how the partner responded.

Daily routines and participation

Morning activities usually begin around 6:45 a.m.. During breakfast, Mateo points toward familiar foods and moves an adult's hand toward containers. He sometimes leaves the table when an item is unavailable. The family will place two choices within view, provide a brief model, and allow time for a response. Adults will acknowledge clear gestures immediately.

Dressing begins around 7:15 a.m.. The child helps push his arms through sleeves when the adult holds the garment open. He has more difficulty when several directions occur together. The family will prepare clothing first and give one direction at a time. A familiar object or gesture will support understanding.

Attendance at The Upside-Down Acorn begins around 8:00 a.m.. The child attends Ms. Lopez's room. Miss Ana assists during meals and outdoor play. Staff report that visual choices and predictable transitions help him remain with the group. Classmates Ivo and Nell often approach him during block play. He watches them, imitates an action, and sometimes takes a desired block without signaling.

Lunch occurs near 11:30 a.m.. Staff will offer an accessible request method before serving additional portions. They will avoid requiring repeated speech attempts when the child's message is already clear.

Evening play often begins around 5:30 p.m.. The sister enjoys drawing suns and naming colors. The Spanish target word "sol" refers to the picture of the sun. The same spoken form is also the sister's name, Sol. Adults will record the context so a picture label is not mistaken for calling a family member.

Developmental and clinical information

The parents report birth at 38 weeks gestation, birth weight 6 lb 11 oz, and Apgar scores of 8 and 9. Delivery occurred at Fernwick River Children's Hospital. These details come from family report and were not independently checked during this review.

The primary physician is Dr. Maren Holt. The family reports no new hospitalization or major medical change. Hearing screening documentation dated March 18, 2026 indicated a pass. The team will request further hearing assessment if new concerns arise.

At the earlier evaluation, the PLS-5 supported a structured description of language performance. The Auditory Comprehension standard score was 78, with percentile rank 7 and confidence interval 73–85. The Expressive Communication standard score was 75, with percentile rank 5 and confidence interval 70–83. The Total Language standard score was 75, with percentile rank 5.

These scores require caution because the child's language experience spans two languages. The team did not use them alone to describe ability or determine priorities. Family interview, observation, and communication across routines provided additional evidence.

During this review, spontaneous productions included "agua", "ma", and "no". A glide resembling [w] occurred in one word attempt. Stable production of /k/ was not observed. Speech sounds are monitored within meaningful communication rather than treated as the main family priority.

Other agencies and community coordination

The family receives nutrition support through Mossvale County WIC. The parents also have an assigned contact at Mossvale County DSS for benefit questions. The team did not review financial records during this meeting.

Mossvale County Partnership for Children provided information about play groups and lending materials. Mossvale County Early Head Start has an application on file. Application status was reported by the mother; enrollment has not been confirmed.

The family identified transportation contact Della Rowan as someone who may help explain available ride arrangements. The coordinator will first clarify the family's need and follow the family's signed information-sharing choices.

With current parent consent, the coordinator may exchange functional communication information with classroom staff. Shared information will describe helpful supports, progress, and barriers. Staff do not need the full clinical record to carry out routine strategies.

The clinician will offer one shared communication page for home and group care. The page will include preferred activities, accepted communication methods, and examples of adult responses. The parents can revise that page whenever routines change.

Outcome 1: Communicate a useful message during meals and play

The family wants Mateo to request an item, more of an activity, or help before distress interrupts participation. Success means a clear gesture, picture selection, sign, or spoken attempt during 4/5 observed opportunities across two familiar routines for two consecutive weeks.

Baseline observation showed clear independent messages in 3/10 opportunities. Most additional requests involved taking an adult's hand or crying. The child responded to brief models with mod cues.

Adults will arrange one natural opportunity at a time. They will keep the desired item visible, pause, and accept an effective response. They will model the target words "más", "agua", and "help" when relevant. Adults will give the item or assistance promptly after the message.

The clinician will use enhanced milieu teaching during family-selected activities and explain each strategy as it occurs. Practice will remain brief. Food, comfort, and necessary care will not depend on producing a word.

The parents and staff will record one example per day when feasible. The clinician will compare independent attempts with attempts that required support and adjust the plan if frustration increases.

Outcome 2: Participate in dressing and cleanup

The family wants the child to complete familiar single-step actions with less repeated talking. Success means participation in 4/5 opportunities with min cues during dressing and cleanup for two consecutive weeks.

Current performance was 2/5 with spoken directions alone and 4/5 when adults added a gesture and familiar materials. This suggests that context and visual support improve access to the instruction.

Adults will use the same short direction for a repeated action. They will wait before repeating it. During dressing, the adult can hold open a sleeve and model the target phrase "arm in". During cleanup, the adult can point to the basket and model "put in".

The family will begin with actions the child already understands. They will add a new action only after the routine becomes easier. Adults will acknowledge participation without requiring eye contact.

The clinician will coach caregivers during the actual routine when possible. Progress notes will state the action, available support, and response. The team will distinguish difficulty understanding a direction from fatigue, discomfort, or refusal.

Outcome 3: Join shared play with another child

The parents want Teo to stay in a simple shared activity and communicate a turn. Success means completing three back-and-forth exchanges in 3/4 opportunities with mod cues or less during familiar play.

Baseline observation included one exchange before the child moved away. Preferred materials included blocks, rolling balls, and animal figures. Adults will begin with a cooperative activity that does not require sharing a highly valued object.

Ms. Lopez will pair him with a willing classmate for a brief activity. The adult will describe whose turn comes next and model the target words "go" or "my turn". Pointing, offering an object, or pushing a ball toward a partner will count as a turn signal.

At home, the sister can participate when she wants to. She will not be responsible for therapy or for preventing distress. Adults will help both children end the activity comfortably.

The clinician will review whether support promotes participation. If the activity repeatedly leads to distress, the team will change the materials, partner, or duration.

Outcome 4: Help communication partners understand emerging words

The family wants familiar adults to recognize speech attempts while continuing to accept other communication methods. Success means partners understand the intended message in 8/10 routine opportunities using the available context and no more than min cues.

The clinician will use focused stimulation with useful words selected by the family. Adults will model a word naturally during an activity without asking for repeated imitation. They will confirm meaning through the object, action, or gesture.

During drawing, the target word "sol" will be documented as a picture label when the child points to a sun. Calling Sol will be documented separately. This distinction matters because the spoken forms match.

A brief language sample will preserve productions such as "a", "tá", and "mo". If analysis uses SALT, an error notation such as [EW] will describe the sample only. It will not replace the family's account of successful communication.

The team will review functional clarity before selecting speech sound targets. Familiar partners will avoid correcting every attempt.

Service plan and dates

Speech-language services will occur once weekly for 45 minutes in the home or group care setting. Services begin October 12, 2026 and continue through April 5, 2027, subject to the IFSP review process.

The usual home appointment is 4:15 p.m. on Mondays. The clinician and family may change the location when another routine offers a better practice opportunity. The clinician will confirm changes directly with the parent.

Each visit will include observation, caregiver practice, feedback, and a brief plan for the week. The family may choose one strategy to practice between visits. Written material will use clear examples rather than technical terms.

The service coordinator will contact the family monthly and help address scheduling, access, and agency questions. Classroom consultation will occur within the authorized service arrangement and existing consent.

Progress will be reviewed on January 5, 2027. The next full IFSP review is planned for April 5, 2027. Earlier review may occur if family priorities, participation, or service needs change.

Agreement and follow-up

The parents agreed that the revised outcomes reflect current priorities. They requested practical examples and brief records of progress. The team will use observations across routines to judge whether support helps the child participate.

The clinician will prepare the shared communication page. The coordinator will confirm transportation options and application status. The family will select the first meal and dressing routine for practice.

This review records family report, direct observation, and team agreement separately. The next visit will establish a comparable baseline for the revised outcomes. No new assessment scores were generated during this review.

Nota diaria de habla y lenguaje

El 8 de octubre de 2026, de 09:10 a 09:55, atendí a Nicolás de la Cruz, de 3;4, en La Nube con Botas Azules, en Brisaloma, Carolina del Norte. Soy Alma Rueda-Linares, patóloga bilingüe del habla y lenguaje de Senderos de Palabras Pediatría. Registré la sesión en el expediente SLP-482731, con Medicaid 683925147Q, autorización AUT-529184 y códigos CPT 92507, modificador GN e ICD-10 F80.2.

Su mamá Elena Carrillo-Santos informó que Nicolás pidió ayuda durante el desayuno. Su papá Julián de la Cruz trabaja en Taller Farol de Cobre. En casa, su hermana Inés participa en juegos de turnos; su abuela Tomasa del Río cuida al niño por las tardes. La familia practica vocabulario al alimentar a su perro Chispa y evita exigir repeticiones cuando aparece frustración.

La maestra Pilar Montalvo observó mayor participación junto a Gael y Luna. La familia asiste al programa de cuentos de Biblioteca Comunitaria Puente de Luciérnagas, donde colabora el voluntario Darío Salcedo. La coordinadora de servicios Celia Arenas mantiene contacto con Oficina CDSA de Brisaloma, DSS del condado de Alcorverde, WIC de Brisaloma, Smart Start de Alcorverde y Early Head Start Semillas del Alba para coordinar transporte, orientación nutricional y apoyos familiares.

Revisé la evaluación del 22 de septiembre de 2026: en PLS-5 Spanish, subprueba Comprensión auditiva, obtuvo puntuación estándar 78, percentil 7, edad equivalente 2;7 e intervalo de confianza 74–84 al 90%. El IFSP del 29 de septiembre de 2026 incluye el resultado 2 y la meta 2.1. Estos datos orientaron las actividades; hoy no administré pruebas estandarizadas.

Durante juego con animales, Nicolás siguió instrucciones en 8/10 oportunidades con apoyos moderados. Produjo combinaciones espontáneas en 3 de 5 turnos. Utilicé estrategias de Hanen y modelado dentro del juego. Para las palabras objetivo "casa" y "gato", trabajamos /k/ y /g/ con apoyos máximos. Dijo "ato" por "gato" y "más agua" sin modelo inmediato. La precisión alcanzó 60%. En la muestra de lenguaje anoté [EW] cuando correspondía.

El niño permaneció atento, aceptó pausas y regresó al juego después de una transición difícil. La participación mejoró cuando ofrecí dos opciones visuales. Su mamá Elena Carrillo-Santos practicó esperar, comentar y ampliar una palabra. Demostró la estrategia con apoyos mínimos. Acordamos usarla durante la merienda y registrar ejemplos breves, sin convertir la rutina en una prueba.

La próxima sesión será el 15 de octubre de 2026. Confirmé el domicilio registrado: 418 Calle del Castaño, Brisaloma, 27903. El contacto familiar es (919) 555-0146 y familia.carrillo@example.org. Los materiales están en https://senderospalabras.example.org/familias. Revisaremos peticiones espontáneas y coordinación con el aula. También observaremos si las combinaciones aparecen durante juego libre y si los apoyos visuales facilitan la transición hacia actividades compartidas.

NOTA DIARIA DE TERAPIA DEL HABLA Y LENGUAJE

Fecha: 10/09/2026. Horario: 09:15 a 09:45.
Paciente: Nicolas Paredes Soto. Edad: 4;2. Nacimiento: 08/09/2022.
Expediente: SLP-2609147. Medicaid: 583206419K.
Diagnostico: F80.2. Servicio: 92507, modificador GN.
Clinica: Servicios Infantiles Puente de Voz.
Profesional: Elena Valverde, patologa bilingue del habla y lenguaje, Carolina del Norte.

S: INFORMACION SUBJETIVA

La madre, Marina Soto, acompanio a Nicolas y explico que pide ayuda con mayor frecuencia en casa. El padre, Andres Paredes, informo por telefono que las dificultades aumentan cuando cambia la rutina. La hermana, Sol, suele responder antes que el paciente. La abuela, Dalia Soto, cuida al paciente despues de clases y desea usar las mismas estrategias.

La familia confirmo domicilio en 184 Calle Sauce Claro, Vallecedro, Carolina del Norte, 27500, condado de Brisamar. Contacto: 919-555-0146; marina.soto@example.com. La madre refirio que el perro, Nube, facilita juegos de turnos. No informo dolor, enfermedad reciente ni cambios de medicamentos. El paciente entro tranquilo y eligio materiales sin dificultad.

O: OBSERVACIONES Y DATOS

La sesion individual se realizo en Escuela Primaria Sendero Azul, perteneciente al Distrito Escolar de Brisamar, en el salon de la maestra Clara Montalvo. La asistente, Ines Robles, observo el cierre. Los companeros Leo Funes y Alma Cordero participaron brevemente durante una actividad de saludo.

Se emplearon Hanen y PECS, con elecciones visuales, espera y expansion verbal. Nicolas siguio instrucciones con dos elementos en 8/10 oportunidades, equivalente a 80%, con apoyo moderado. Identifico acciones en 3 de 5 oportunidades con apoyo minimo. Produjo solicitudes espontaneas en 60% de las oportunidades y dijo "quiero agua", "dame carro" y "mas burbujas".

Para el objetivo /k/, se practicaron las palabras "casa" y "copa". La precision fue 6/10 con apoyo maximo. Se observo [ [KEEP] ] como anotacion pendiente; la transcripcion confirmada fue [w] durante una imitacion aislada. La muestra de lenguaje incluyo el codigo [EW].

La evaluacion previa, fechada 09/18/2026, correspondio a 92523. En PLS-5 Spanish, Comprension auditiva obtuvo puntuacion estandar 77, percentil 6, intervalo de confianza 72-84 y edad equivalente 3;0. Comunicacion expresiva obtuvo puntuacion estandar 79. Estos resultados se revisaron con la madre.

A: ANALISIS CLINICO

Nicolas mostro mejor participacion cuando el adulto presento una instruccion y espero su respuesta. Las ayudas visuales facilitaron la comprension; las preguntas consecutivas redujeron las respuestas espontaneas. La precision articulatoria aumento despues del modelo, pero todavia depende de ayudas directas.

El rendimiento respalda continuar la intervencion para lenguaje receptivo y expresivo. Los datos actuales describen esta sesion y no sustituyen una nueva evaluacion. La madre practico una expansion y pudo repetir la estrategia sin ayuda. Se recomienda que Sol espere antes de contestar por el paciente.

P: PLAN Y COORDINACION

Continuar el objetivo del IFSP 2.1, establecido el 09/25/2026, mediante solicitudes funcionales durante juego y merienda. Practicar diariamente con materiales familiares y registrar respuestas independientes.

Se reviso el plan con Paula Neri, coordinadora de servicios de Agencia Comunitaria de Coordinacion Familiar del Valle, abreviada ACCFV. La oficina de referencia es Oficina de la Agencia de Servicios de Desarrollo Infantil de Vallecedro, denominada CDSA Vallecedro. La familia dispone del portal https://cdsa-vallecedro.example/seguimiento.

Proxima sesion: 10/16/2026, a las 09:15. Firma: Elena Valverde.

Se revisaron registros previos: Rossetti, aplicado a los 26 meses; Bayley, puntuación escalar 7; y Peabody, puntuación estándar 83, percentil 13. La participación mejoró cuando el adulto siguió sus intereses y ofreció tiempo de espera. Persisten dificultades para organizar frases espontáneas y mantener sonidos posteriores.
