text:
BILINGUAL PEDIATRIC SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION  
Synthetic clinical record: all people, organizations, identifiers, and events in this document are fictional.

Client: Elian Bellacampo Monteluna  
Preferred name: Lito; chart initials: E.B.M.  
Date of birth: August 3, 2022  
Evaluation date: October 5, 2026  
Chronological age: 4;2  
Session: 9:15 a.m.–11:05 a.m.  
Record number: SLP-2601005-482  
Medicaid member number: 902641735Q  
Authorization: NC-SL-68420319  
Parents: Lucía Monteluna and Omar Bellacampo  
Home address: 418 Mossbell Lane, Wrenhollow, North Carolina 27000  
Telephone: (919) 555-0146  
Parent email: lucia.monteluna@example.com  
Preschool: The Lantern Marmot Atelier  
Referring pediatrician: Dr. Cora Velazul  
Evaluating bilingual speech-language pathologist: Nerea Valdemonte, MS, CCC-SLP  
Clinician’s employer: Piedmont Moonbridge Communication Partners  
Clinic address: 72 Fernspindle Court, Wrenhollow, North Carolina 27000  
Clinic telephone: (984) 555-0128  
Clinic website: https://moonbridge-communication.example  
Evaluation procedure: CPT 92523  
Treatment procedure proposed: CPT 92507, modifier GN  
Diagnostic impressions: ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0

**Antecedentes y motivo de consulta**

Elian was referred because his family and classroom staff report difficulty understanding his speech and helping him explain events. His mother described him as affectionate, curious, and quick to notice changes in routines. She stated, “Él sabe lo que quiere, pero cuando no le entendemos, se frustra.” The family wants him to request help, participate in play, and describe a problem without an adult guessing the full message.

Both parents attended the interview. Lucía Monteluna used Spanish for most family history and switched to English when discussing school routines. Omar Bellacampo used both languages throughout the visit. The clinician completed direct assessment in Spanish and English. Interpreter Alma Juniper assisted with a brief discussion involving an English-speaking scheduling staff member and checked the parents’ understanding of administrative forms. She did not translate or administer standardized test items.

The family first requested support after teacher Ms. Maribel Quillcrest reported that Lito often watched classmates before following a spoken direction. Assistant teacher Mr. Jonas Reedvale noted that he communicated more readily during outdoor play. Their written observations described short spoken messages, frequent gestures, and difficulty answering questions about something that had already happened. They also described strong interest in pretend cooking, wheeled toys, and songs with predictable movements.

At The Lantern Marmot Atelier, children move among an art room, a garden area, and small play groups. The unusual preschool name refers to its classroom lantern collection and a fictional animal mascot. Elian attends morning sessions. His parents reported that arrival goes smoothly when staff show him the activity board. An unexpected room change can lead him to hold an adult’s hand and repeat "¿dónde?" until someone explains the next activity.

Referral information came from Willowbend Child Development Services Agency. Service coordinator Tessa Alderwick provided an earlier IFSP dated May 12, 2025. The document listed IFSP outcome 2 for functional communication during family routines and IFSP outcome 4 for participation in play. The family reported that services ended during the transition to preschool. Current eligibility and service arrangements require confirmation through the responsible local programs.

This assessment combined parent interview, teacher information, observation, standardized testing, and supported learning tasks. The purpose was to describe communication across languages and identify useful supports. The clinician explained that bilingual development does not itself cause a language disorder. Differences between Spanish and English sound patterns must be considered before classifying an error. The report separates observed performance from information reported by the family or other providers.

**Historia de nacimiento, salud, familia e idiomas**

According to his parents, Elian was born at Fernhaven Women’s and Children’s Hospital in Briarfen, North Carolina, on August 3, 2022. Gestational age was 38 weeks, 4 days, and birth weight was 6 lb 9 oz. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. His mother described an uncomplicated delivery and routine discharge. These details came from parent report; the original birth record was unavailable during this evaluation.

The family reported no major surgery, seizures, prolonged hospitalization, or known neurological diagnosis. Elian had several ear infections during early childhood. Dr. Cora Velazul documented a referral for hearing assessment after the most recent episode. Audiologist Brenna Willowmere completed testing at Fernhaven Children’s Hearing Center on September 18, 2026. The supplied summary described hearing responses within expected limits and recommended follow-up if new concerns arise.

Early motor development was described as somewhat uneven. Independent walking began at 16 months, and consistent spoken words emerged around 20 months. His parents recalled more frequent word combinations by 31 months. These ages are retrospective estimates. His father explained, “We remember the first words because he named the dog, pero las frases llegaron despacito.” There was no reported loss of previously established speech, social engagement, or motor skills.

Occupational therapist Imani Fenwick sees Elian through Pebblepath Pediatric Therapy Collective. Her summary describes difficulty with clothing fasteners, variable tolerance for sticky textures, and improved participation when activities have a clear ending. Physical therapist Theo Maraviel previously assessed balance and stair use. The family reported that ongoing physical therapy was not recommended. Neither provider’s observations establish the cause of the communication concerns, but they help explain participation during unfamiliar tasks.

Feeding history includes a limited range of preferred textures and reluctance to try mixed foods. The parents reported comfortable drinking, chewing of familiar foods, and no recent coughing during meals. Sleep varies when household work schedules change. During the session, Elian appeared alert and comfortable. The clinician observed adequate movement for the speech tasks attempted. This visit did not include an instrumental swallowing assessment or a comprehensive examination of oral structure.

The household includes his mother, father, older sister Sol, and younger brother Will. Grandmother Luz Campoverde provides care after preschool. Aunt Paz Monteluna helps with transportation, and babysitter Dalia Fernlace stays with the children when work shifts overlap. The family’s dog, Nube, frequently appears in pretend-play stories. His mother reported that he gives the dog elaborate gestures even when his spoken explanation remains brief.

The parents described several current and former workplaces because their schedules affect attendance. His mother works at Brindle Basket Store, which she calls la tienda Brindle Basket. She previously worked at Silver Heron Restaurant, el restaurante Silver Heron, and accepts occasional shifts through Morning Thimble Cleaning Service, el servicio de limpieza Morning Thimble. She prefers appointment reminders by text because she cannot reliably answer telephone calls during a shift.

His father works at Copper Wren Plant, la planta Copper Wren. His previous seasonal employment included Blue Acorn Farm, la finca Blue Acorn, and weekend work with Stone Lantern Construction Company, la compañía de construcción Stone Lantern. The parents emphasized that these changes reflect available work, not changes in the child’s primary caregivers. They requested appointments that can remain consistent even when either parent has a different shift.

Spanish is the main language used by the parents and grandmother. His sister Sol often uses English during games and Spanish during meals. His brother Will hears both languages. The family estimated current exposure at approximately 65% Spanish and 35% English, with variation across the week. These estimates describe opportunities to hear language. They do not measure proficiency, and neither language should be reduced solely because communication is delayed.

During family gatherings, cousins Rosa Bellacampo and Teo Monteluna usually speak Spanish with him. At preschool, classmates Milo Embernook and Yara Quillhaven generally speak English. His parents reported that Elian follows familiar play routines in either language. He has more difficulty when a partner introduces a new rule or asks for an explanation. Familiar partners often interpret his gestures before he needs to complete the spoken message.

His mother’s concern was not that he mixed languages. She stated, “En casa decimos things in both languages, y eso está bien; lo difícil es que no puede contar qué pasó.” His father agreed that he wants the child to communicate with grandparents and teachers. The family identified telling someone about pain, asking another child to stop, and explaining a missing toy as priorities. These functional concerns guided the interpretation and recommendations.

**Evaluación y resultados / Assessment findings**

Elian entered the room holding his mother’s hand and inspected the toy shelf before approaching the clinician. He initially answered through pointing and brief speech. After a predictable play routine began, he initiated exchanges and brought materials to the adult. He accepted transitions when shown the next item. Participation decreased during longer verbal tasks and improved after movement breaks. The assessment therefore used several short blocks rather than one continuous testing period.

The clinician administered PLS-5 Spanish using its bilingual procedures. Spanish items were presented as directed, with permitted English opportunities when appropriate. The score table records performance obtained under those procedures. Additional teaching, repetitions beyond permitted limits, and picture choices were documented separately. The clinician did not combine supported responses with standardized scores. Results remain one part of the assessment because language exposure, attention, and familiarity with testing affect how a child demonstrates skills.

| Measure or subtest | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish: Auditory Comprehension | 79 | 8th percentile | 90% confidence interval: 73–87 | 3;5 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Expressive Communication | 76 | 5th percentile | 90% confidence interval: 70–84 | 3;2 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Total Language | 76 | 5th percentile | 90% confidence interval: 71–83 | 3;3 |

The PLS-5 Spanish results suggest weaknesses in understanding and producing language relative to the test reference group. The Total Language standard score of 76 must be interpreted with the broader bilingual findings. Age equivalents are descriptive test values, not an estimate of the child’s overall developmental age. They should not determine classroom placement, replace functional observations, or imply that all communication skills occur at one developmental level.

On Auditory Comprehension, Elian identified familiar objects, understood routine action words, and followed simple directions within an established activity. He had difficulty with less familiar location concepts, sentences containing multiple details, and questions requiring an inference. He sometimes selected the last item named. When the clinician changed the order of choices, his response changed too. This pattern suggests that some incorrect responses reflected incomplete processing rather than lack of interest.

During a separate supported task, he followed related two-step directions in 3 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Performance improved to 5 of 5 with mod cues, gestures, and a visual sequence. Spanish directions involving "debajo" and "detrás" were less consistent than directions involving "en". Similar difficulty occurred with English targets "under" and "behind". This cross-language pattern supports concern about the underlying concepts.

On Expressive Communication, he named familiar objects and produced short combinations to request, comment, and protest. He used verbs but often omitted information needed to identify who completed an action. His descriptions relied on the immediate context. When asked about a pictured event, he said "niño cae" and pointed to the ground. With an adult model, he expanded this to "el niño se cayó", showing useful responsiveness to support.

A conversational sample collected during pretend cooking and vehicle play included Spanish, English, and mixed utterances. Examples included "más juice aquí", "yo want ese", and "carro go rápido". These productions demonstrate flexible use of available vocabulary. Code-switching itself was not scored as an error. The clinician examined whether each message conveyed a clear meaning and whether omissions also appeared in productions made entirely within one language.

The sample was annotated using selected SALT conventions. Unintelligible whole utterances received [EU], and unintelligible words within otherwise understandable utterances received [EW]. The clinician retained both languages in the transcript and did not translate productions before examining them. The sample was too limited and too dependent on adult support for a meaningful comparison with a monolingual database. It nevertheless showed recurring difficulty extending messages beyond the immediate shared activity.

Speech production was examined through GFTA-3 picture prompts, spontaneous speech, and Spanish word probes. Because the English task was used descriptively and included adaptations, no norm-referenced speech score was reported. Sounds-in-Words responses helped identify patterns for further examination. Errors were checked against Spanish phonology, English exposure, and consistency across repeated attempts. An English sound difference was not classified as disordered merely because it differed from the clinician’s English production.

Observed patterns included omission of some final consonants, reduction of consonant clusters, and inconsistent substitution of front sounds for back sounds. For target "casa", he produced "tasa". For target "gato", he produced "dato". He also used [w] in some English words containing /ɹ/. That substitution was interpreted cautiously because English /ɹ/ differs from Spanish /ɾ/ and has a different developmental course.

The clinician elicited /k/ in isolation in 8/10 trials with mod cues. Accuracy decreased to 3/10 in simple syllables with min cues. Production of /g/ was less consistent. He watched the clinician’s mouth and responded to a playful contrast between target "casa" and his production "tasa". This brief task suggests that supported sound learning is possible, although it does not establish independent use in conversation.

The clinician understood approximately 70% of words in the contextual play sample. His mother understood approximately 90% during the same activity. These estimates reflect different familiarity and access to context; they are not standardized intelligibility scores. Understanding decreased when he described an event the listener had not seen. His mother occasionally asked him to show the item, after which she supplied an interpretation that the clinician could not independently confirm.

During a short story task, Elian identified the main character and an obvious action. He did not independently explain the problem or connect the ending to the earlier event. After dynamic assessment with picture sequencing and models, he described the problem in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. He retained part of the sequence after a brief break. This learning response supports intervention that combines clear models with meaningful repeated practice.

Social communication included shared attention, showing objects, turn-taking, and checking an adult’s reaction during play. He protested when a desired toy was unavailable and accepted an alternative after an explanation. He rarely repaired a misunderstood message through additional words without support. Instead, he repeated the original production more loudly or moved closer to the object. Repair improved when the adult offered a choice between showing, pointing, and trying another phrase.

Teacher information described similar difficulties during group activities. Ms. Maribel Quillcrest reported that Yara Quillhaven sometimes answered for him. Mr. Jonas Reedvale observed more independent speech when Milo Embernook waited before taking a toy. The clinician recommends protecting that response time. Peer assistance can support inclusion, but routine answering on the child’s behalf may hide his communication needs and reduce opportunities to practice an independent message.

**Impresiones clínicas**

Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, ICD-10 F80.2, with a co-occurring speech sound disorder, ICD-10 F80.0. The conclusion rests on converging evidence: parent concerns, teacher observations, difficulties across both languages, structured assessment, and reduced functional clarity. Bilingual exposure does not explain the full pattern. The child shows difficulty understanding and formulating messages even in familiar Spanish routines with supportive communication partners.

Speech differences require continued monitoring as vocabulary and connected speech expand. Some English productions may reflect Spanish influence or limited experience. Other patterns affect familiar words in both languages and reduce understanding. Intervention should therefore target the patterns with the clearest functional effect and the strongest evidence of difficulty. The current assessment does not support treating every English sound difference as a separate error or requiring identical performance across languages.

Strengths include social interest, pretend play, purposeful gestures, willingness to imitate within play, and improved performance with visual support. Elian notices communication breakdowns and seeks adult help. His family already provides rich interaction in Spanish and English. These strengths make daily routines useful settings for treatment. The goal is a clearer, more complete message while preserving his access to both languages and his connection with family members.

Interpretive limits include the relatively short observation period, parent-reported developmental history, and the descriptive use of English speech prompts. Attention varied across activities. The score table cannot capture every skill or predict the exact rate of progress. The clinician recommends reassessment through treatment data, classroom observations, and family feedback. Any later change in hearing, health, or participation should prompt review of how that change affects communication.

**Recomendaciones / Plan compartido**

1. Begin bilingual speech-language treatment through Piedmont Moonbridge Communication Partners after scheduling and authorization are confirmed. Use CPT 92507 with modifier GN when appropriate for the authorized service. Initial treatment should address functional language and speech clarity through play and family routines. Record performance separately for independent responses and responses requiring min cues, mod cues, or max cues so progress remains clear.

2. Target understanding of related directions, location concepts, and questions about familiar events. A proposed goal is following related two-step directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues across repeated sessions. Use objects and actions before moving to pictures. Practice concepts in Spanish and English as they naturally occur. Avoid assuming that successful repetition means the child understands the direction.

3. Support longer, more informative messages through focused stimulation, expansions, and recasts. Adults can acknowledge the message and add one useful detail. For example, after "carro go", model target "el carro va rápido" or target "the car goes fast", depending on the interaction. Allow the child to respond without requiring an immediate imitation every time.

4. Teach communication repair during genuine misunderstandings. Practice target "otra vez", target "te enseño", and target "help me say it". The proposed criterion is using a repair strategy in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Pictures can supplement speech when needed. Coordinate the same choices across home and preschool so the child does not need to learn a different system in each setting.

5. Address speech patterns through phonological contrast therapy, beginning with carefully selected familiar words containing /k/ and /g/. Consider Cycles if later sampling confirms several persistent patterns affecting clarity. Do not select English /ɹ/ as an initial priority based only on this visit. Measure carryover in meaningful words and connected speech, rather than relying only on successful imitation in isolation.

6. Continue speaking Spanish at home and use English when it fits the family interaction. Neither parent needs to replace a comfortable language with a less comfortable one. During meals, dressing, and shared books, pause after a comment and allow a response. Babysitter Dalia Fernlace and grandmother Luz Campoverde can use the same brief models. Siblings should remain play partners rather than assume responsibility for correcting speech.

7. Share this report with Dr. Cora Velazul, occupational therapist Imani Fenwick, and preschool staff through the family’s chosen release process. Review progress on January 11, 2027. Contact the hearing provider if new listening concerns develop. Ask Willowbend Child Development Services Agency to clarify transition records and current program contacts. No external transmission occurred as part of this fictional assessment.

The parents stated that the plan reflects their priorities. Lucía Monteluna summarized, “Queremos que pueda decir lo que necesita, con sus palabras.” Omar Bellacampo requested a short home practice note in both languages. The clinician provided examples and asked the parents to identify routines that feel manageable. Treatment planning will build from those routines and adjust according to the child’s response, family feedback, and classroom participation.

Bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, North Carolina

REPORTE DE EVALUACIÓN DEL HABLA Y LENGUAJE / SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION

This fictional report contains invented people, organizations, locations, contacts, and clinical findings. It is intended for offline de-identification testing.

DATOS DEL CLIENTE / CLIENT INFORMATION

Field	Information
Client	Emilio Rafael Valverde
Preferred name	Milo
Date of birth	August 8, 2022
Evaluation date	October 8, 2026
Report date	October 10, 2026
Chronological age	4;2
Parent/guardian	Mariela Valverde
Other parent	Tomás Valverde
Home address	418 Lantern Finch Lane, Cedar Vale, North Carolina 27864
County of residence	Juniper Bend County
Medical record	CV-260108-472
Medicaid member number	683927451M
Referral authorization	SLP-26-88419
Evaluation service	92523
Proposed treatment service	92507
Requested modifier	GN
Provisional diagnosis	F80.2
Clinician	Daniela Mireles, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist
Employer	Lantern Finch Pediatric Speech and Language Therapy, PLLC
Clinic location	92 Willow Lantern Court, Suite B, Cedar Vale, North Carolina 27864

CONTACTOS / CONTACT TABLE

Role	Name or organization	Contact
Mother	Mariela Valverde	(252) 555-0148
Father	Tomás Valverde	252-555-0163
Family email	Mariela Valverde	mariela.valverde@example.com
Evaluating clinician	Daniela Mireles	252.555.0182
Therapy office	Lantern Finch Therapy	intake@lanternfinch.example
Therapy website	LFPSLT	https://lanternfinch.example
Pediatrician	Dr. Rebeca Nolasco	+1 252 555 0117
Preschool teacher	Ms. Anabel Cárdenas	252 555 0134
Grandmother in Mexico	Elvira Valverde	+52 55 0000 0146

MOTIVO DE REFERENCIA / REASON FOR REFERRAL

Dr. Rebeca Nolasco referred Emilio for concerns about understanding classroom directions, combining words, and explaining needs during peer activities. His mother reported that communication becomes harder when adults speak quickly or when several people talk together. She stated, “En casa sabemos lo que quiere, pero afuera se queda calladito.” His father described frequent pointing, repeated attempts, and occasional frustration when listeners misunderstand.

The family requested an evaluation that considers Spanish and English together. They wanted practical guidance for home and preschool, especialmente para que pueda pedir ayuda sin llorar. The referral did not request accent reduction or replacement of the home language. The family identified participation, communication repair, and more independent language as priorities.

Milo attended with his mother. The visit began at 9:15 a.m. and ended at 10:45 a.m., including movement breaks and caregiver discussion. His father joined briefly by telephone at 10:20 a.m.. The clinician obtained information through caregiver interview, preschool records, structured tasks, play observation, and language samples. Results describe performance during this visit and require interpretation alongside daily communication.

ANTECEDENTES / BACKGROUND

Emilio Rafael Valverde attends Little Orchard Bridge Preschool in Cedar Vale. He previously attended Nido de Colibrí Daycare in Bellfern. Preschool staff reported that he enjoys blocks, pretend cooking, and outdoor play. He watches classmates before entering an activity and often follows their actions when spoken directions are unclear.

Ms. Anabel Cárdenas reported that classmates Nora Bellamy and Isaac Montel frequently invite him to play. He sometimes gives objects to Nora without explaining the intended game. When Isaac changes the plan, he may protest through gestures or leave. Classroom assistant Rosa Melgar stated that pictures and a brief demonstration improve participation.

The family moved within North Carolina before enrollment. His mother reported no prolonged interruption in caregiving. She explained, “El cambio de escuela fue grande; ahora conoce las rutinas, pero todavía necesita tiempo.” The clinician considered this adjustment when interpreting classroom participation. Quiet behavior with unfamiliar adults did not automatically indicate lack of knowledge.

An earlier referral through Juniper Bend Child Development Services Agency generated case JB-CDSA-22167. The archived plan dated June 12, 2025 included IFSP outcome 2, which addressed requesting help during family routines. The agency closed that record after transition planning. No active agency service was confirmed during this evaluation.

HISTORIA DE NACIMIENTO Y SALUD / BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

His mother reported delivery at Bellfern Regional Women and Children’s Hospital on August 8, 2022. Gestational age was 38 weeks, 4 days, and birth weight was 3.12 kg. Reported Apgar scores were 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. These details came from the caregiver’s discharge summary.

The pregnancy reportedly included routine prenatal care and mild maternal anemia. His mother denied significant delivery complications. He stayed with his mother after birth and did not require intensive care. Feeding initially involved breast milk and later mixed feeding. The family reported no persistent swallowing concern, choking pattern, or poor weight gain.

Medical history includes seasonal congestion and several episodes of middle-ear fluid. Dr. Nolasco referred him to audiologist Esteban Rivas at Willowcrest Children’s Hearing Center. An audiology summary dated September 18, 2026 documented responses adequate for conversational speech and recommended monitoring if ear symptoms return. The clinician reviewed the summary; she did not perform a diagnostic hearing examination today.

The family reported independent walking at 14 months and first consistent words near 19 months. Two-word combinations became more frequent around 33 months. His mother recalled early words in both languages. She did not report loss of previously established skills. He currently uses familiar phrases more reliably than spontaneous explanations.

Sleep varies when congestion increases. The family reported no seizures, major surgery, or daily prescription medication. Pediatric follow-up remains with Dr. Rebeca Nolasco. Oral structures appeared adequate for observed speech and feeding activities. This observation does not replace dental, medical, or swallowing assessment. No feeding evaluation was requested or completed.

FAMILIA E IDIOMAS / FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Emilio lives with his parents and sister Alina Valverde, age 7 years. Spanish is the main language used by adults at home. His sister frequently uses English during games, luego cambia al español cuando él no entiende. The parents support both languages and want him to communicate with relatives without depending on translation.

His mother, Mariela, works at Puentes de Papel Family Literacy Cooperative, a fictional nonprofit. The family also attends its weekend library program, Puentes de Papel Cuentos en Familia. Activities include shared books, crafts, and songs. Program volunteer Berta Solano knows the family and provides books with pictures that support conversation.

His father, Tomás, works at Bellfern Lantern Fabrication. He speaks Spanish during meals and English during some construction games. He stated, “No queremos dejar el español; queremos que tenga más palabras en los dos idiomas.” The clinician supported continued use of each caregiver’s most comfortable language.

Grandmother Elvira speaks Spanish during video calls from Mexico. Aunt Lidia Valverde visits regularly and helps with transportation. Cousins Camila Solís and Bruno Solís join family play on weekends. Their mother reported that the cousins sometimes answer for him, aunque él todavía está tratando de decirlo. Adults were encouraged to provide time before helping.

Babysitter Yadira Ponce provides care after preschool. She speaks Spanish and uses familiar English phrases from classroom routines. The family’s dog, Chispa, often appears in spontaneous conversation and pretend play. His mother noted that stories about Chispa produce longer utterances than questions about school.

Caregivers estimated greater exposure to Spanish overall, with English concentrated in preschool and sibling play. These estimates describe opportunities, not proficiency. The clinician did not assume balanced bilingual development. Language mixing was expected and was not counted as an error by itself. Vocabulary was considered across both languages when the task allowed conceptual scoring.

PROCEDIMIENTOS / ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES

The clinician administered selected components of the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish and obtained structured speech probes. The PLS-5 Spanish results below are synthetic clinical data. Standardized tasks followed the designated bilingual administration sequence. Additional teaching, repetition, and alternative wording occurred separately and did not change the reported standardized scores.

The Auditory Comprehension subtest examined understanding of vocabulary, concepts, relationships, and increasingly complex directions. The Expressive Communication subtest examined naming, word combinations, grammar, and verbal explanation. The Total Language score summarized performance across the two subtests. Scores alone do not establish a diagnosis.

A conversational sample included pretend shopping, animal play, picture description, and discussion of a recent family outing. The clinician used Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts conventions for selected observations. The sample was too brief for a normative comparison. Codes supported description of errors and communication repair within the observed interaction.

Dynamic tasks examined response to brief teaching through Graduated Prompting. The clinician first offered an independent opportunity, then used min cues, mod cues, or max cues as needed. The evaluation also included caregiver coaching and observation of transfer to a new activity. Supported performance was reported separately from independent performance.

RESULTADOS / STANDARDIZED SCORE TABLE

Measure or subtest	Standard score	Percentile	Confidence interval	Age equivalent
PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension	76	5th percentile	90% CI: 71–84	3;1
PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication	73	4th percentile	90% CI: 68–81	2;11
PLS-5 Spanish Total Language	73	4th percentile	90% CI: 68–80	3;0

Age equivalents provide limited descriptive information. They do not mean that every skill matches a younger child’s development. Confidence intervals reflect uncertainty around the reported scores. Interpretation also considered bilingual exposure, observed function, caregiver concerns, and response to support.

COMPRENSIÓN / RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE

Emilio identified familiar objects and understood routine action words in both languages. He followed a familiar direction when the materials and adult’s gesture made the task clear. Understanding decreased when directions included a location concept, an unfamiliar adjective, or several actions without contextual support.

He identified pictured actions in 8/10 opportunities, or 80%, with min cues. He followed novel two-part directions in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. For location words, performance was 4/10 independently and 7/10 after a model. The targets included “under”, “behind”, “debajo”, and “detrás”.

He sometimes selected the most familiar object rather than following the full sentence. For example, when two animals differed by size and location, he attended to the animal name but missed the relationship. A shorter sentence and visual demonstration helped. This pattern also appeared during Spanish tasks, suggesting that English exposure alone did not explain the difficulty.

His mother’s use of familiar wording improved attention, but did not remove all errors. The clinician observed stronger understanding during meaningful routines than during isolated questions. This strength can support treatment, provided that practice gradually includes new materials and communication partners.

EXPRESIÓN / EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE

Spontaneous language included short combinations, gestures, sound effects, and memorized social phrases. Milo used both languages within the same interaction. Mixing languages preserved meaning in several utterances. The clinician evaluated sentence organization and communication function without treating every switch as an error.

Observed productions included “quiero blue carro”, “dog se fue”, “mami help aquí”, and “yo no puedo open”. These examples communicated clear intent. Longer explanations often omitted information that an unfamiliar listener needed. He pointed to clarify rather than adding a description.

During picture description, he named a character or action but rarely linked them independently. After a model, he produced “el niño está comiendo” and later generalized to “la niña está tomando”. He maintained the structure with mod cues, then shortened it when the picture changed. Immediate imitation was stronger than independent transfer.

Requests included “más”, “otra vez”, and “my turn”. For an unfamiliar container, he said “abre” while handing it to his mother. When the clinician paused, he added “abre caja”. This showed useful emerging expansion, especially when adults provided time instead of supplying the whole message.

Selected sample entries received the [EW] code for extraneous words under the chosen transcription conventions. Spanish words within mixed utterances did not receive [EW] solely because they were Spanish. The clinician reviewed context before assigning codes and did not use the codes as an independent diagnostic measure.

HABLA Y PARTICIPACIÓN / SPEECH AND PARTICIPATION

Speech was easiest to understand in short, familiar messages. Longer utterances contained omissions and substitutions that reduced clarity. The clinician heard variable production of /k/ and /g/ in both languages. Spanish /ɾ/ was inconsistent. English /ɹ/ sometimes sounded like [w].

A probe of /k/ showed 6/10 correct productions independently and 8/10 with mod cues. For the target “casa”, he produced “tasa” before achieving the initial sound with support. For “car”, he produced “tar”. These observations require broader sampling before a separate speech diagnosis.

Voice and fluency appeared functional during the available sample. He shared enjoyment, sought his mother’s attention, and accepted turn-taking with support. Frustration increased when an adult misunderstood repeatedly. He recovered after a brief pause and a choice of communication options. No single behavior was interpreted outside its interactional context.

IMPRESIONES / CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, provisionally coded F80.2. Difficulties affected understanding of novel directions, independent sentence expansion, and communication repair across Spanish and English. Caregiver reports, classroom observations, and structured findings converged. Bilingual development and language mixing did not adequately explain the full pattern.

Emilio showed strengths in social interest, familiar vocabulary, imitation, and learning with visual support. He responded to brief teaching and participated longer when tasks had a clear purpose. These strengths support a favorable treatment response, although the rate of progress cannot be predicted from one visit.

Speech sound differences may add to communication difficulty. A separate speech sound diagnosis remains deferred pending a larger bilingual sample and monitoring. The clinician also recommends continued hearing follow-up when symptoms occur. The present evaluation does not establish a broader developmental diagnosis or replace a multidisciplinary assessment.

RECOMENDACIONES / PLAN DE SERVICIOS

Begin individual bilingual speech-language treatment through Lantern Finch Pediatric Speech and Language Therapy, PLLC. Use functional play, family routines, and preschool activities. Initial intervention should include Enhanced Milieu Teaching and Focused Stimulation, with caregiver practice between visits. Spanish should remain available throughout treatment.

SERVICE SCHEDULE / HORARIO PROPUESTO

Service	Frequency	Duration	Location	Planned start	Usual time	Code
Individual bilingual treatment	Twice weekly	Thirty minutes	Lantern Finch Therapy	October 20, 2026	3:30 p.m.	92507 with GN
Caregiver coaching	Within each treatment visit	Ten minutes included	LFPSLT	October 20, 2026	3:50 p.m.	Included
Preschool consultation	Monthly	Twenty minutes	Little Orchard Bridge Preschool	November 5, 2026	11:15 a.m.	Per authorization
Plan review	After the initial treatment block	Forty-five minutes	Lantern Finch Therapy	January 12, 2027	4:00 p.m.	Clinical review

Authorization SLP-26-88419 remains subject to payer confirmation. The proposed schedule does not document completed visits.

METAS INICIALES / INITIAL GOALS

Goal 1: During meaningful play, follow novel two-part directions with 80% accuracy across consecutive sessions, using no more than min cues. Provide opportunities in both languages and report performance by language and support level.

Goal 2: Produce an expanded message containing an action and relevant information in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Accept meaningful bilingual combinations. Targets may include “quiero el carro grande” and “the dog is sleeping”.

Goal 3: Repair a communication breakdown through repetition, added words, gesture, or a picture in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Teach functional options such as “ayuda, por favor”, “I mean this one”, and “otra vez”.

Goal 4: Establish a broader bilingual speech sample and monitor production of /k/, /g/, and /ɾ/. Add sound-specific treatment only when the pattern, functional impact, and language expectations support it.

PRÁCTICA EN CASA Y ESCUELA / HOME AND SCHOOL SUPPORT

1. Follow his interest during play. Describe the action with a short sentence, pause, and allow him to respond. Expand his message by adding useful information without requiring repeated imitation every time.

2. Offer choices that create a reason to communicate. Place desired materials within view, then wait. Accept speech, gesture, or a picture, and model a fuller message after acknowledging his intent.

3. Read familiar picture books in either language. Comment before asking questions. Revisit the same pages and connect pictures to daily routines. The family can continue attending Puentes de Papel Cuentos en Familia for enjoyable language opportunities.

4. Coordinate classroom supports with Ms. Cárdenas and assistant Melgar. Give brief directions, show the first action, and check understanding through performance. Allow extra response time during group activities.

5. Invite classmates Nora Bellamy and Isaac Montel into predictable turn-taking games. Adults should model useful phrases and gradually reduce help. Avoid asking peers to interpret every message.

6. Share the same routines with babysitter Yadira Ponce and aunt Lidia Valverde. During family play, encourage sister Alina and the cousins to wait before answering for him.

CIERRE / CAREGIVER DISCUSSION

The clinician reviewed results with Mariela Valverde in Spanish and English. She summarized the plan as “darle tiempo, hablar claro y seguir usando nuestros dos idiomas.” Her summary matched the main recommendations. The family agreed to begin treatment and requested preschool coordination after the required release is completed.

Daniela Mireles, MS, CCC-SLP
Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist
Lantern Finch Pediatric Speech and Language Therapy, PLLC

BILINGUAL SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION / EVALUACIÓN BILINGÜE

- **Client:** Mateo Julián Salcedo Rivera, called Teo at home. Date of birth: June 4, 2022. Age at evaluation: 4;2. Pronouns: he/him.
- **Evaluation:** August 10, 2026, from 9:15 a.m. to 11:00 a.m.. Report completed: August 14, 2026. All people, organizations, identifiers, events, and findings in this document are fictional.
- **Caregivers:** mother, Guadalupe Marisol Rivera, also called Lupita; father, Jesús Andrés Salcedo, also called Chuy.
- **Residence:** 2846 Lanternberry Lane, Willowmere, North Carolina 27863, in Bellhaven County.
- **Clinician:** Elena Sofía Valdés, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, Puentes Pediatric Communication Services. Referral provider: Dr. Camila Rojas.
- **Administrative identifiers:** Medicaid ID 846291735M; insurance member ID NCF-582604193; former NC ITP child ID ITP-BH-220674; clinical record SLP-260810-047; authorization AUTH-82645109.
- **Contact:** (919) 555-0146; intake@puentes-pediatric.example; https://puentes-pediatric.example.

MOTIVO DE CONSULTA / REASON FOR REFERRAL

- The family requested evaluation because Mateo often needs adults to interpret his messages. His mother reported, “En casa habla más, pero cuando no le entienden, se queda calladito.” She wants him to explain discomfort, join classroom play, and ask for help without becoming upset.
- The referral described difficulty understanding longer directions and producing complete sentences across languages. The school also reported reduced speech clarity during unfamiliar activities. This evaluation addressed language learning, speech production, functional communication, and the effect of language access on participation.
- The family did not request that English replace Spanish. Their priority is communication con confianza in both languages. The clinician explained that bilingual exposure itself does not establish a disorder. Findings were considered across home reports, classroom examples, direct observation, and supported teaching.
- Caregivers identified successful communication as a message understood by the intended listener, whether spoken in Spanish, English, or a combination. They also wanted practical strategies that fit their work schedules and existing routines.

BACKGROUND / ANTECEDENTES

- Teo lives with both parents and two siblings. His grandmother provides regular care after preschool. The family moved within the same county before the current school placement. Caregivers described stable housing, predictable meal routines, and several adults available for transportation.
- Earlier records show participation in the North Carolina Infant-Toddler Program through Bellhaven Children’s Developmental Services Agency. Service coordinator Nora Beltrán supported the family. The initial IFSP was dated August 19, 2024, when the child was 26 months.
- Former IFSP outcome 3 addressed requesting assistance during daily routines. The discharge summary dated June 3, 2025 described increased use of gestures and short spoken combinations. Those records did not include comparable bilingual testing, so present findings cannot establish a standardized change over time.
- The family reported that communication improved when adults slowed the exchange and showed the object being discussed. Difficulty persisted when a listener could not see the activity. Caregivers asked for recommendations they could share across home, school, and community settings.

HISTORIA DE NACIMIENTO / BIRTH HISTORY

- Pregnancy history was obtained from the mother and a supplied discharge summary from Willowmere Regional Birth Center. Delivery occurred on June 4, 2022, at 6:42 a.m.. Gestational age was 38 weeks, 4 days, and birth weight was 3.12 kg.
- Apgar scores were 8 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. The mother reported no neonatal intensive care admission. The discharge summary described routine newborn observation and feeding support. These statements reflect the available fictional record and caregiver account.
- Early feeding included breast milk and formula. The family recalled a comfortable transition to mashed foods at 7 months and table foods at 12 months. They did not report persistent choking, painful swallowing, or difficulty maintaining growth.
- Reported developmental milestones included independent sitting at 7 months, walking at 14 months, and consistent meaningful words near 20 months. Caregivers recalled that gestures developed before spoken combinations. These milestone ages are retrospective estimates and were not independently measured.

HISTORIA MÉDICA / MEDICAL HISTORY

- Primary care is provided by Dr. Camila Rojas at Bellhaven Family Children’s Clinic. The mother reported recurrent middle-ear infections during toddlerhood. No ear tubes, seizures, major surgery, or current daily medication were reported.
- Audiologist Samuel Ibarra completed an assessment on July 16, 2026. The supplied summary documented hearing adequate for access to speech during that visit. Caregivers were advised to seek medical follow-up if hearing behavior changes or infections recur.
- Occupational therapist Maya Chen previously addressed tolerance for grooming and transitions. Services ended on May 22, 2026, according to the supplied discharge note. The present evaluation did not assess motor skills or establish the need for renewed occupational therapy.
- Sleep varies with the household work schedule. The mother described occasional waking and said, “Si durmió poquito, necesita más tiempo para contestar.” No sleep diagnosis was supplied. During this visit, the child remained alert and participated with brief breaks.
- Feeding concerns were not observed during the snack routine. The child managed the offered textures without obvious distress. This observation was limited and does not replace a feeding or swallowing evaluation.

FAMILIA Y LENGUAS / FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

- Mother Guadalupe Marisol Rivera uses mainly Spanish with the children. Mom works nights as a packaging technician at Lantern Grove Medical Packaging. Father Jesús Andrés Salcedo works as a maintenance assistant at Bellhaven Orchard Apartments and uses both languages.
- Older brother José Emiliano Salcedo Rivera, called Pepe, usually speaks English during games. Younger brother Juan Manuel Salcedo Rivera, called Juanito, hears mainly Spanish during caregiving routines. The siblings frequently switch languages together.
- Maternal grandmother Rosa Elena Rivera provides afternoon care. Aunt Inés Maribel Rivera helps with transportation. Babysitter Daniela Cruz follows the family’s Spanish routines. Their dog, Canela, often joins play and provides a familiar conversation topic.
- Caregiver estimates placed daily language exposure at approximately 60% Spanish and 40% English. These percentages describe reported exposure, not measured proficiency. English exposure increases during school days, while Spanish remains central to family stories, comfort, and discipline.
- The family attends a play program at Casa del Roble Community Center. Program leader Maribel Santos offers bilingual songs and crafts. The parents value this setting because the child can participate without pressure to use only English.

ESCUELA Y PARTICIPACIÓN / SCHOOL PARTICIPATION

- Mateo attends Juniper Lantern Elementary School in Bellhaven Creek Public Schools. He participates in the Sunflower classroom with Ms. Adriana López and classroom assistant Mr. Daniel Reed.
- Classroom reports describe strong interest in blocks, vehicles, and pretend cooking. He approaches classmates Lucía Paredes and Tomás Vega during familiar play. Friend Emma Solís sometimes helps explain his message, which supports participation but can limit independent communication.
- Ms. López reported that visual routines improve follow-through. Spoken directions become harder when they contain unfamiliar vocabulary or several actions. The teacher noted that the child sometimes watches another student before beginning, making comprehension difficult to judge from task completion alone.
- During group activities, Teo contributes more when an adult previews the topic. He may answer with a gesture, one word, or a short mixed-language phrase. Classroom staff reported that communication difficulty is most noticeable during disagreements and unexpected changes.
- The family authorized sharing this report with the educational team. Recommendations below address access and participation. Eligibility decisions require the school’s own process and review of educational impact.

PROCEDIMIENTOS / ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES

- The clinician completed caregiver interview, record review, play observation, speech sampling, oral mechanism screening, and a bilingual language sample. PLS-5 Spanish tasks provided structured information. Auditory Comprehension and Expressive Communication items were considered alongside functional performance.
- Selected administration procedures required added demonstrations, repeated directions, and acceptance of responses across languages. These changes limit direct comparison with the test’s normative sample. Scores below are descriptive training data and should not be treated as independent diagnostic proof.
- A SALT-style transcript supported qualitative review of utterance length, vocabulary, and communication repairs. The sample contained 50 utterances. It was collected during vehicles, picture description, snack preparation, and pretend shopping.
- The clinician used test–teach–retest activities to examine response to instruction. Supports included visual examples, extra processing time, and min cues, mod cues, or max cues as documented. No separate interpreter participated because the clinician conducted the visit in Spanish and English.

OBSERVACIONES / BEHAVIORAL OBSERVATIONS

- Mateo entered holding his mother’s hand and watched the materials before approaching. He selected the toy garage, checked his mother’s face, and began play after the clinician demonstrated a simple routine. Engagement increased when the activity had a clear purpose.
- The child used eye gaze, pointing, speech, and facial expression together. He accepted turn-taking with familiar materials. During difficult tasks, he sometimes moved an item toward the adult instead of explaining what he needed.
- Spanish prompts generally produced faster responses during family routines. English responses increased during school-related play. Code-switching occurred naturally within sentences and did not consistently coincide with errors or loss of meaning.
- A movement break and snack supported sustained participation. The mother described the observed behavior as typical for an unfamiliar appointment. No major distress prevented assessment, although unfamiliar vocabulary and repeated testing demands affected performance.
- The clinician separated nonresponse from an incorrect response when possible. A quiet response could reflect uncertainty, processing demands, or limited comfort. Conclusions therefore rely on patterns across tasks rather than silence during a single item.

RESULTADOS / SCORE TABLE

- The following table records the fictional structured results. Confidence intervals are included for documentation practice. Because administration included additional supports, interpret every value with the stated limitations.

  | Measure | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th percentile | 90% CI: 73–85 | 3;3 |
  | PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication | 75 | 5th percentile | 90% CI: 70–83 | 3;0 |
  | PLS-5 Spanish Total Language | 75 | 5th percentile | 90% CI: 71–82 | 3;1 |

- Age equivalents describe performance on particular test items. They do not represent the child’s overall developmental age, learning potential, or appropriate classroom placement.
- Informal familiar-object identification was 8/10 without added support. Novel two-action directions were completed in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Sentence expansion improved from 2/6 to 5/6 after teaching.
- These findings show a benefit from support and continued difficulty with unfamiliar language. The table must remain connected to the bilingual observations, family priorities, and classroom reports.

COMPRENSIÓN / RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE

- Teo identified common objects and understood familiar actions in either language. He followed routine directions most readily when the relevant materials were visible. Understanding decreased when the instruction required remembering several details without a visual reference.
- Spatial words were inconsistent across languages. For the target "under", he initially placed the vehicle beside the box. After demonstration of "debajo", he completed 4/5 related trials with min cues. The improvement suggests that teaching and context supported comprehension.
- Questions about a visible event were easier than questions about an absent event. He responded to the target "who", or "quién", more consistently than explanatory questions. When asked the target "why", or "por qué", he often repeated an action word.
- Longer directions should be divided into meaningful steps while adults check understanding. Repeating the same sentence more loudly did not improve performance. Showing the action, reducing competing language, and allowing processing time provided more useful support.
- Difficulty appeared in both languages when task demands increased. Limited English exposure alone did not account for the full observed pattern.

EXPRESIÓN Y MUESTRA / EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE SAMPLE

- The child communicated requests, comments, protests, and invitations. He used short combinations more often than connected explanations. During play, productions included "quiero carro blue", "se cayó ahí", and "I need más". These mixed-language messages were meaningful in context.
- Utterances sometimes omitted information the listener needed. For example, "ese no", without a clear gesture, did not identify the unwanted item. With mod cues, he revised the message to "no quiero ese carro". Repair improved when the adult named the missing information.
- During picture description, "boy fall", "niña está come", and "him running", reflected difficulty with grammatical forms. Such examples were considered within each language. Code-switching itself was not counted as a grammatical error.
- Transcript annotations included [EW] for an extraneous word and [EU] for an utterance requiring contextual interpretation. These codes supported analysis only. They do not identify a diagnosis, and the same production was not counted repeatedly across categories.
- The child learned a modeled sentence pattern during play and later used it with a different object. However, independent explanations remained brief. Caregivers reported similar difficulty describing school events when pictures or shared context were unavailable.

HABLA / SPEECH PRODUCTION

- Speech clarity varied with sentence length, listener familiarity, and context. Caregiver estimate of intelligibility to familiar listeners was 80%. The clinician understood approximately 60% of connected speech without contextual support. These are informal estimates.
- Observed productions included "tat", for target "cat", and "tasa", for target "casa". Errors involving /k/ occurred in both languages during the sample. Other productions included [w] for /ɹ/ in English and variable production of Spanish /ɾ/.
- Some differences reflected the sound systems of the two languages. The clinician did not treat every cross-language difference as an error. Persistent patterns affecting familiar words and everyday clarity received greater weight than isolated productions.
- With a visual model and mod cues, the child produced /k/ in 6/10 syllable attempts. Performance decreased in connected speech. This response supports further work on stimulability and functional sound practice without establishing a motor speech diagnosis.
- Oral screening showed adequate movement for observed tasks. No consistent voice concern was heard. Fluency interruptions were occasional and did not include obvious struggle during this sample.

IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS / CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

- Findings support concern for a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and reduced speech sound accuracy. The clinical record lists provisional ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0. These impressions remain subject to follow-up and coordination with the educational team.
- Evidence includes difficulty across languages, limited independent explanations, reduced clarity, and functional impact reported at home and school. Modified standardized results contribute descriptive information but do not determine the impressions alone.
- Strengths include social interest, purposeful gestures, engagement in pretend play, supportive caregivers, and a positive response to teaching. The child benefits from adults who recognize Spanish, English, and mixed-language communication as valid.
- The evaluation does not establish cognitive ability, autism, hearing disorder, or motor speech disorder. Those questions require appropriate assessment if new concerns arise. Current recommendations address the communication needs documented in this visit.

RECOMENDACIONES / RECOMENDACIONES

- Begin bilingual speech-language intervention, with frequency adjusted to participation and progress. Use focused stimulation, recasts, and milieu teaching within meaningful play. Consider Cycles for persistent sound patterns after a broader bilingual speech inventory.
- Teach useful messages for requesting help, explaining a problem, and joining play. Keep target vocabulary relevant to both home and school. Accept either language while providing models that fit the language of the activity.
- Coach caregivers during brief routines. The mother requested activities después de la cena, because daytime practice is difficult after night shifts. Use shared play, dressing, and snack preparation. Caregivers should pause, acknowledge the message, and offer one useful expansion.
- Provide classroom visuals, preview unfamiliar vocabulary, and check understanding through action or explanation. Avoid relying only on a yes response. Support direct exchanges with peers while allowing adults to help when communication breaks down.
- Former IFSP outcome 3 may inform the new plan, but current goals should reflect preschool demands. Proposed goal 1 addresses communication repair in 4/5 opportunities with min cues. Proposed goal 2 addresses two-action directions in 80% of supported opportunities.
- Review progress on November 13, 2026. Proposed goal 3 addresses selected speech targets in 8/10 meaningful practice opportunities with mod cues. Adjust targets using bilingual samples and caregiver feedback.
- The evaluation service is documented under CPT 92523, modifier GN. Treatment planning may use CPT 92507, modifier GN, subject to the actual authorization terms.
- Signed electronically by Elena Sofía Valdés on August 14, 2026. The family received an oral Spanish summary and an English report with Spanish examples. No external transmission occurred as part of this fictional document.

+ Name: María José Cárdenas Villaseca
+ CA: 4;2
+ DOB: 08/06/2021
+ Evaluation date: 10/09/2025
+ Report date: 10 de octubre de 2025
+ Context: Bilingual pediatric speech-language evaluation; caregiver interview, structured assessment, play, and conversational sampling
+ Languages: Spanish and English
+ Examiner: Marisol Estrada Peña, MS, CCC-SLP
+ Employer: Juniper Bridge Pediatric Communication
+ Location: Briarcombe, North Carolina
+ Record: JBPC-2025-04718
+ Medicaid member: 482761935Q
+ Authorization: AUTH-73190426
+ Referral: Elena Robledo, MD
+ Billing: CPT 92523; modifier GN
+ Document status: Fictional clinical record for software testing

Resumen / Evaluation Summary

María José participated in a bilingual evaluation with her mother and later joined the clinician for play. She showed strong interest in pretend cooking, picture books, and helping adults organize materials. Her communication included gestures, short phrases, and longer messages when the topic was familiar. Spanish was her stronger language during storytelling and family discussion; English appeared frequently during classroom routines and toy play.

Findings support difficulty understanding longer directions and organizing spoken messages across both languages. Speech sound patterns also reduced clarity, especially in longer words. These findings reflect information from several settings and do not rest on an English score alone. The family’s language practices provide useful communication resources. Continued use of Spanish at home is recommended.

Her mother described the main concern this way: “Ella sabe lo que quiere decir, pero se queda buscando las palabras.” The evaluation identified strengths that can support treatment: shared attention, persistence, symbolic play, and willingness to try again when an adult gives clear support.

Motivo de consulta / Background

The referral dated 09.18.2025 requested assessment because adults sometimes misunderstood classroom messages and the child had difficulty following group instructions. Her mother, Lucía Villaseca Romero, reported that familiar listeners usually understand the topic but may need gestures to understand details. Her father, Rafael Cárdenas Soto, described frustration when several people speak at once: “Conmigo conversa tranquila; en grupo se apura y ya no le sale igual.”

María José attends The Lantern Otter Learning Grove in the mornings. She also receives preschool support through Mossbank County Schools at Willow Finch Elementary School. She joins the Acorn Room with Miss Ana Mejía. Classroom assistant Mr. Tom helps with transitions and outdoor play.

The teacher reported that she follows familiar routines, watches other children before starting unfamiliar tasks, and rarely volunteers a full explanation during circle time. She often plays beside Nadia Solís and seeks Benji Mercado for pretend restaurant games. Staff requested practical ways to support participation without requiring her to repeat every message.

Historia de nacimiento y salud

The family reported birth at Silver Heron Regional Hospital in Alderwick, North Carolina, on 6 de agosto de 2021. Gestational age was 38 weeks, 4 days, and birth weight was 3.12 kg. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. Delivery occurred by cesarean section after labor did not progress. The mother reported no prolonged breathing support, neonatal infection, or feeding tube.

Early feeding involved breastfeeding and bottle feeding. The family described a gradual transition to textured foods, with temporary refusal of mixed textures. Current meals include familiar family foods. No coughing, choking, unexplained weight loss, or persistent wet voice was reported. Feeding was discussed through interview and was not directly assessed.

The child reportedly sat independently at 7 months and walked at 14 months. First meaningful words appeared around 18 months, and regular word combinations emerged near 30 months. The family sought early intervention at 26 months.

Records from Mossbank Infant and Toddler Connections included an IFSP dated 3 de marzo de 2024, with outcome 2 addressing communication during meals and play. Service coordinator Irene Valdés documented a review on el martes 4 de junio de 2024. The family reported that services ended after preschool transition.

Pediatric follow-up occurred on 2025-08-21. Audiologist Daniela Ponce at Silver Heron Regional Hospital documented hearing adequate for speech access on 08/28/2025. No current medication or known seizure history was reported.

Familia e historia lingüística

The family lives at 4186 Wren Hollow Lane, Briarcombe, North Carolina 27864, in Mossbank County. Household members include both parents, sister Alma Cárdenas Villaseca, and brother Diego Cárdenas Villaseca. Her maternal grandmother, doña Lupe, provides afternoon care. An aunt, Teresa Villaseca Romero, helps with transportation. The family’s dog, Canela, often joins play routines.

Spanish is used for meals, family stories, discipline, and most conversations with adults. English is common in preschool activities, songs, and sibling games. Her sister sometimes translates classroom phrases, aunque la familia prefiere que cada adulto hable directamente con la niña. The father works at Paloma Orchard Packing Cooperative and reported using both languages at work.

The mother grew up in Dos Alisos, Mexico. She described several family varieties of Spanish and asked that regional vocabulary remain acceptable in treatment. No language loss was reported. The family wants the child to communicate comfortably with relatives and teachers, “sin tener que escoger un solo idioma.”

The grandmother reported that María José tells longer stories when looking at family photographs. Babysitter Rosa Téllez described similar strengths during familiar play.

Procedimientos y observaciones

The appointment began at 9:15 a.m. and ended at 11:05 a.m., with a movement break and snack. The clinician conducted the interview in Spanish and offered English when discussing school forms. No interpreter was needed. The child selected materials, watched demonstrations, and remained engaged when tasks had a clear endpoint.

Assessment included PLS-5 Spanish, a descriptive administration of selected GFTA-3 items, and a bilingual language sample using SALT conventions. For PLS-5 Spanish, the clinician followed bilingual administration procedures. Additional teaching probes occurred after scored items and did not change standardized scores. English articulation results were interpreted descriptively because the available norms do not represent this child’s complete language experience.

A quiet room supported individual testing. The child initially whispered, then increased her volume during pretend play. She accepted redirection and asked for help through pointing, eye contact, and speech. Fatigue became noticeable near the final picture tasks. The clinician documented responses before offering min cues, mod cues, or max cues during separate probes.

The mother confirmed that observed vocabulary and sentence patterns resembled home communication. Classroom reports were reviewed alongside direct observations.

Resultados / Score Table

| Measure | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish: Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th percentile | 90% interval: 73–85 | 3;2 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Expressive Communication | 76 | 5th percentile | 90% interval: 71–83 | 3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Total Language | 75 | 5th percentile | 90% interval: 70–82 | 3;1 |

Age equivalents describe performance on these tasks and should not be treated as the child’s overall developmental age. Confidence intervals reflect measurement uncertainty. The results require interpretation with language exposure, functional participation, and response to teaching.

Comprensión y expresión

During Auditory Comprehension tasks, the child identified familiar objects, actions, and basic spatial relationships. She had difficulty retaining directions with several elements and interpreting sentences that changed the order of people or actions. She sometimes selected the last object named, especially when pictures contained several plausible choices.

During Expressive Communication tasks, she named familiar items and combined words to request, describe, and protest. Longer responses often omitted information that a listener needed. Spanish verb forms and English sentence structure varied, but errors were interpreted in context rather than counted automatically as evidence of impairment.

In play, María José produced "yo want agua", "la bebé está sleepy", and "he go allá". Code-switching itself was appropriate to the interaction. Difficulty appeared when she could not explain who acted, what happened, or why.

After a brief model, she followed novel directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues, compared with 4/10 independently. She added a missing event in 3 of 5 picture sequences with mod cues. This response suggests benefit from structured teaching.

Habla / Speech Sound Findings

The descriptive GFTA-3 sample and Spanish play sample showed several recurring speech patterns. The child sometimes replaced /k/ with [t] and /g/ with [d]. She reduced consonant clusters in longer words and occasionally used [w] for English /r/. Spanish /ɾ/ was inconsistent. These patterns were reviewed against language-specific expectations and the family’s pronunciation models.

Examples included "tasa" for "casa", "pato" for "plato", and "poon" for "spoon". Some differences reflected developing bilingual speech patterns; recurring substitutions across languages had a clearer effect on intelligibility.

The clinician understood approximately 72% of words in the contextual play sample. Familiar listeners reported higher understanding. Accuracy improved during imitation with mod cues, especially when the clinician slowed the model and paired it with a visual gesture.

Oral structures appeared functional during informal observation. Voice quality and speech fluency did not raise concerns during this visit.

Pragmática, juego y participación

The child shared enjoyment, offered pretend food, and checked whether the listener was watching. She initiated interaction more often during play than during direct questions. She repaired communication by pointing or showing an object, aunque a veces repetía la misma frase sin agregar información.

In a classroom account, la maestra Ana described a disagreement over toy dishes. María José tried to explain the event but needed help naming the other child and stating what happened first. The teacher reported that classmates remained interested when adults supported turn-taking.

The child described school transport assistant Ernesto Saldaña through his role and a gesture. She needed a model to explain the complete event. This observation supported a focus on message organization and repair strategies.

Impresiones clínicas

The combined findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder affecting participation across Spanish and English. Proposed diagnostic codes are ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0. The clinician based these impressions on functional concerns, bilingual assessment, speech samples, and observed response to teaching.

Limited English exposure alone does not explain the difficulties described in Spanish. At the same time, the evaluation does not classify code-switching or regional Spanish forms as errors. The child showed meaningful learning potential when adults reduced task demands and gave specific models.

This evaluation represents one visit. Classroom observation and treatment data should refine priorities. Hearing documentation supports access to spoken instruction, but the family should report any new hearing concerns. Prognosis for improved functional communication is favorable with coordinated support.

Recomendaciones / Plan

1. Begin bilingual speech-language therapy weekly, with caregiver participation. Use CPT 92507 and modifier GN when appropriate. Select activities from family routines and classroom needs.

2. Establish goal 1: follow directions containing two linked actions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Confirm understanding through action, rather than requiring verbal repetition.

3. Establish goal 2: describe a short event with the person, action, and relevant detail in 4 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Accept either language and natural code-switching.

4. Establish goal 3: improve production of selected speech targets to 80% accuracy during meaningful play with mod cues. Begin with stimulable sounds and words that affect daily understanding.

5. Use focused stimulation, expansions, and recasts during play. Consider Cycles for persistent phonological patterns after collecting a broader speech sample. Explain each approach to caregivers in their preferred language.

6. Support communication repair with modeled phrases such as "te enseño", "I mean this one", and "otra vez, más despacio". Praise successful clarification without requiring perfect pronunciation.

7. Continue Spanish at home. Encourage shared books, cooking conversations, and family stories. Parents can respond naturally in the language they use most comfortably.

8. Coordinate classroom supports with Miss Ana. Pair directions with pictures, allow processing time, and provide a model before group storytelling. Offer predictable chances to speak with peers.

9. Review progress after a treatment block. Track functional participation alongside task accuracy. Discuss school eligibility through the district’s own evaluation process.

Seguimiento y contacto

The family scheduled a planning call for 10/16/2025 at 4:30 p.m.. Contact information is (919) 555-0137 and lucia.villaseca@example.org. The clinician’s office uses (984) 555-0118, marisol.estrada@example.com, and https://juniperbridge.example.org/familias.

The mother requested a Spanish summary for doña Lupe and classroom suggestions in English. Copies are intended for the family and authorized school staff. Release arrangements will be documented before distribution.

Signed: Marisol Estrada Peña, MS, CCC-SLP  
Juniper Bridge Pediatric Communication  
Signature date: 10/10/2025

During snack play, the child requested through pointing, reaching, or a vocal attempt in 6/10 opportunities with min cues. At home, sister Sol enjoys pretend kitchen play; pt joins briefly when she offers a spoon. Family dog Chispa sometimes interrupts floor play. CG will move play materials away from the dog’s resting area.

Evening bath begins near 7:15 PM. Dad described bath play as the easiest routine for shared attention. Weekend library visits are variable; family prefers practicing during ordinary errands before adding another scheduled activity.

**Otras agencias y recursos**
